Zájmena {he}/{his}/{him}/{He}/{His} podle vojáka.
items: a photograph gone soft at the edges
a book with the last pages torn out
a lock of hair in a matchbox
a pack of cards missing the queen of hearts
a child's drawing of a horse
a pocket Bible with a hole in it
a key to a house that is no longer there
enlist: {name} came up the line with {item} and nothing else. The sergeant wrote {him} down as {rank} and pointed at the mud.
Nobody saw {name} arrive. One morning there was simply one more helmet in {sector}, and a quiet {archetype} under it.
{name} signed the papers with a steady hand. The trench at {sector} took {him} in like it takes everyone: without a word.
They issued {name} a rifle, a spade and a number. {He} kept {item} in {his} breast pocket, where the shrapnel would have to go through it first.
{name} arrived with the evening ration party, carrying {item} and a borrowed coat two sizes too big.
The new {archetype} gave {his} name as {name}. The corporal looked at {his} boots, then at the mud, and laughed for the first time in a week.
{name} stepped off the supply cart at {sector} and stood very still, listening to the guns as if they were saying {his} name.
Nobody asked {name} why {he} came. Nobody in {sector} asks that. {He} was handed a spade before {he} was handed a rifle.
{name} took the place of a man nobody would talk about. The dugout still had his blanket. {He} kept it folded.
{name} reported to {sector} with {item} sewn into {his} tunic lining. The sergeant pretended not to notice.
{name} was a {trade} in {home} until the posters went up. {He} came to {sector} with {item}, and within a day the whole squad knew that {he} {quirk}.
In {home}, {name} was a {trade}. In {sector}, {he} is a number and a rifle. {He} has told everyone {he} intends to be a {trade} again.
{name} left {waiting} behind in {home} and came up the line with {item}. The men noticed at once that {he} {quirk}.
The new {archetype} is {name}, once a {trade} from {home}. The corporal asked if a {trade} was any use in a trench. {name} said {he} would find out.
{name} told the sergeant {he} was a {trade}. The sergeant said the war needed one of those like it needed a hole in the roof, and put {him} on sentry.
{name} came from {home}, where there is a river, a church and no mud at all. {He} talks about all three as if they were people.
{name} arrived at {sector} with a carefully folded uniform. The first low beam ruined the cap; the first puddle ruined the rest.
At the depot, {name} had practised answering to {his} name. At {sector}, the first person to call it only wanted help with a crate.
{name} reached {sector} expecting a speech. The welcome consisted of a mug, a space on a bench and directions to the latrine.
The quartermaster asked {name} to sign for the blanket. {He} examined the blanket and asked whether the holes were included.
{name} unpacked {item} at {sector}. The man in the next bunk shifted his bag to make room without asking what it was.
{name} introduced {him}self as a {trade} from {home}. The corporal repeated the name correctly. That helped more than the advice.
On the way to {sector}, {name} tried to memorise every turn. By the dugout door, {he} was simply glad someone else knew the way.
{name} found a place in {sector} between a snorer and a man who talked in his sleep. The available alternative was under the leak.

daily.text: Rain all night. {name} bailed water out of {sector} with a helmet until {his} hands stopped feeling anything.
{name} wrote a letter home. {He} wrote about the weather. {He} did not write about the rats.
On sentry duty {name} watched the wire for six hours. Twice {he} thought the wire watched back.
A flare lit {place} like noon. {name} counted the seconds until darkness: eleven.
{name} carried duckboards up from the rear all night. {His} shoulders are a map of splinters.
In reserve, {name} slept nine hours in a barn. {He} dreamt of nothing, which was the best part.
{name} traded {item} for two cigarettes and immediately regretted it.
The cook's stew tasted of iron and smoke. {name} ate two helpings anyway.
{name} spent the night underground, listening. Somewhere beneath {place} someone else was digging too.
{name} carried three men out of {sector} on a stretcher. One of them thanked {him}. Two could not.
{name} ran a message through the communication trench under shellfire. The message said: 'Hold.'
{name} lay in the ruins of {place} from dawn to dusk. {He} did not fire once. That is also a kind of victory.
{name} buried two men at the edge of {place} and said the words twice, because the shells interrupted the first time.
{name} cleaned the gun for the fourth time today. The gun is the only thing in the trench that is kept dry.
{name} made soup from what the rats left. The men called it the best soup on the front, and they were not joking.
A shell landed close to {sector}. When the dust settled {name} was still there, holding {item}, laughing without sound.
{name} found a flower growing out of a sandbag. {He} did not tell anyone. {He} checks on it every morning.
A crow sat on the parapet above {name} all afternoon. The men say it chose {him}.
The rain did not stop once. {name} slept standing up, wedged against the wall of {sector}, and dreamt of dry socks.
{name} lost a boot to the mud at {sector}. It took two men and a rifle sling to get it back. The mud kept the sock.
Water rose to the second step of the dugout. {name} moved {item} to the highest shelf and sat beside it like a guard.
Fog so thick that {name} could not see the end of {his} own rifle. Somewhere out there, someone was whistling.
In the fog a figure walked along the parapet of {sector}. When {name} challenged it, there was nobody there.
The fog lifted at noon and {name} saw {place} clearly for the first time. {He} wished it had stayed.
Frost on the wire made it sing in the wind. {name} could not stop listening to it.
{name} woke with {his} hair frozen to the sandbags. The cook brought tea so hot it hurt. Nobody complained.
The mud froze hard overnight. For one morning {name} could walk on top of it, like a man walking on water.
A clear sky. {name} kept {his} head low all day: on clear days the snipers do not miss.
Sun on {sector}. {name} took off {his} boots for the first time in nine days and the whole squad applauded.
Clear night. {name} counted stars until a flare went up and drowned them all.
Lightning lit {place} and {name} saw the enemy wire, the enemy trench, and a man in it looking straight back.
Thunder all night. {name} flinched at every crack. The old hands said that is how you spot the new ones. By morning, they were flinching too.
The east wind brought the smell of the other trenches: smoke, lime and somebody's cooking. {name} was hungry and furious about it.
The wind tore a sheet of corrugated iron off the dugout roof at {sector}. {name} chased it halfway down the communication trench.
{name} spent the night filling sandbags. By dawn {he} could no longer close {his} hands. By noon the shells had emptied half of them again.
{name} had a letter from home. {He} read it four times and then once more out loud, for the men who never get any.
A rat stole {name}'s cheese ration while {he} watched. {He} let it. The rat looked hungrier.
{name} was on wiring party in no man's land. Every time a flare went up {he} froze like a scarecrow. It worked.
{name} lost at cards to the corporal and now owes him a week of tobacco and one favour, unspecified.
Rumour reached {sector} that the war would be over by spring. {name} has heard it before. So has everyone.
{name} carved {his} initials into the trench wall next to a hundred others. Some of them are only half finished.
{name} spent the afternoon delousing {his} shirt over a candle. The lice won on points.
{name} sang under {his} breath on sentry. Across the wire, very quietly, somebody sang the next line.
A shell hit the latrine at {sector}. Nobody was hurt. {name} says it was the best day of the war.
Officers came to inspect {sector}. {name} polished {his} buttons with mud, which is the only polish there is.
{name} found an old map of {place} from before the war. There was a school on it, and an orchard. {He} looked for them. {He} did not find them.
{name} turned a year older today. The whole squad sang for {him}, badly, and the cook found a candle.
{name} saw a hare run the whole length of no man's land and nobody on either side fired at it.
{name} stood at the parapet at dawn with the rest of {sector}, bayonet fixed, staring into the grey. Nothing came. Nothing came yesterday, either.
Listening post, three in the morning. {name} heard boots, then whispering, then nothing. Just a fox, the corporal said. {He} did not sleep afterwards.
A trench raid went out from {sector}. {name} waited at the gap in the wire, counting heads as they came back.
{name} hauled ammunition boxes up the communication trench all night. {His} back filed a formal complaint.
{name} repaired a collapsed wall of the trench at {sector} with sandbags, boards and language not fit for letters home.
Behind the lines {name} had a bath in a beer vat with eleven other men. The water was brown before {he} got in.
In the rear quarters, {name} played football against the sappers. The ball was a sandbag stuffed with straw. The sappers cheated.
{name} drew the counter-mine plans by candlelight. Below {place} the earth is now a maze, and {he} knows every turn.
{name} set a charge under the enemy listening post. Then {he} waited all night for an order that did not come.
{name} splinted a broken leg with a rifle and two belts. The patient asked if {he} was a real doctor. {He} said yes. {He} was lying.
The aid post ran out of morphine at four. {name} held a boy's hand until six. Then {he} went back for the next one.
{name} ran six messages in one night. The last one was a request for more runners.
{name} took the long way round {place} because the short way had a sniper on it. The long way had two.
{name} spent the day watching one loophole in the enemy line. At dusk a periscope rose in it. {He} let it go. Tomorrow.
{name} moved {his} hide three times today. Snipers who stay in one place do not stay anywhere for long.
The machine gun jammed at the worst moment. {name} cleared it with a bent nail and words the chaplain pretended not to hear.
{name} fired three short bursts at nothing to keep the enemy honest. The enemy fired three back to keep {him} honest too.
The telephone wire to {sector} was cut by shelling four times. {name} crawled out and spliced it four times.
{name} sent a pigeon back to headquarters. The pigeon came back two hours later. {name} took it personally.
{name} flashed a lamp signal to the battery behind the ridge. The answer came back: a single word, misspelled.
The cook's fire went out. {name} relit it under {his} own coat and served stew that tasted of wool.
{name} carried hot tea up to the front line in petrol cans. Everyone could taste the petrol. Everyone drank it.
{name} held a service in a shell hole. Eleven men came. Two of them had never prayed before. Both of them asked for another.
{name} wrote letters for men who could not write, and some for men who could but did not know the words.
{name} studied the trench map until the candle died, then walked {sector} in the dark to learn it by heart.
{name} had orders to attack at dawn. {He} wrote back asking for artillery first. The orders were cancelled. Nobody knows which of {his} words did it.
{name} censored the men's letters tonight. {He} crossed out the place names and left in all the love.
{name} wrote to {waiting}. {He} did not mention the shelling. {He} mentioned the stars.
Someone in {sector} asked {name} about {home}. {He} talked for an hour. Nobody interrupted.
{name}'s hands still remember being a {trade}'s hands. Today they mended a broken duckboard as if it were the most important job in the world.
The men have learned that {name} {quirk}. Tonight it made them laugh, which was worth a great deal.
A letter reached {name} from {home}. The streets there still have names. {He} read them out loud, one by one.
{name} dreamt {he} was back in {home}, working as a {trade}. {He} woke up and said nothing all morning.
{name} {quirk}. Today, under fire at {place}, that habit was the only steady thing in {sector}.
Asked what {he} will do after the war, {name} said: 'Be a {trade} in {home}. And never complain about anything, ever again.'
A replacement turned out to be from {home} too. {name} and the newcomer argued about the same bakery for half the night.
{name} thought about {waiting} on sentry tonight, and the night felt a little shorter.
The corporal found out {name} used to be a {trade}. {name} has been doing two jobs ever since.
{name} found a shirt button in the bread. {He} ate around it and kept the button. Both were useful.
The parcel for {name} contained six left socks. By supper, {he} had found three men willing to trade.
{name} tried to describe the smell of {home} and got as far as the bakery. Then the ration cart arrived.
A borrowed pencil wore down while {name} was writing home. The last line is twice as large as the first.
{name} shaved using a spoon for a mirror. One side looks ready for inspection. The other looks ready for winter.
The bread was divided with a ruler. {name} received the smallest piece and the job of looking after the ruler.
{name} spent an hour repairing a pocket. Nothing goes in it now without a careful inspection.
Someone had labelled the water bucket 'Soup'. {name} changed it back after lunch, too late to settle the argument.
The shelling stopped while {name} was counting the seconds between hits. {He} kept counting anyway, and waited a long time before moving.
A newspaper reached {name} with the corner torn off. According to the half a sentence that survived, the war was going well.
{name} dreamt about missing a train. Waking up here felt like a harsh punishment for it.
{name} traded for a better blanket and got a reputation as a sharp dealer. The man who lost it wants a rematch.
{name} tried to write home with gloves on. The address is readable. Everything else will need some imagination.
{name} found a clean spot on the table and set {his} bread on it. Within a minute, someone asked to borrow the spot.
Somebody hung a doorbell on the next dugout. {name} went to look. It was a spoon tied to an empty tin.
Asked what {he} wanted after the war, {name} said a chair. After some thought: a chair nobody else was sitting on.
{name} heard wire rattling beyond the parapet. At the change of watch, {he} said exactly where and asked for it to be taken seriously.
{name} drew the street leading to {home}. There was no room left for the last house, so {he} turned the page over.
The men argued about whether fish sleep. {name} said yes, and was told to explain how anyone could know.
A bullet hit the sandbag beside {name}. {He} ducked, and noticed {his} hands were shaking. {He} kept working anyway.
{name} saved half a biscuit for later. Later came six minutes afterwards.
The cook asked for an honest opinion of the stew. {name} asked if second helpings depended on the answer.
{name} brushed dried mud off a letter and found one more word under it: 'soon'. {He} wished the rest of the sentence had survived.
The patrol came back one man at a time. {name} held the gap open and counted until the corporal said that was everyone.
{name} made a list of things to buy on leave. It started with socks and ended with a meal nobody could call a ration.
New laces made {name}'s boots look almost respectable, until {he} stood up.
{name} watched a pale shape beyond the wire while a flare burned out. It turned out to be a sack, right where the sack had always been.
A parcel from home held a comb. {name} has hardly any hair left after the last haircut, but {he} appreciated the thought.
An unexploded shell lay beside the approach trench. {name} helped steer the carrying party around it and was glad to leave the problem to somebody else.
An empty jam tin became {name}'s cup. The first drink still tasted of strawberries. {He} took small sips.
{name} remembered the tune but not the words. Six men offered six different songs, and none of them helped.
The gas alarm sounded during supper. {name} put the bread down carefully and did not finish it until the all-clear.
{name} washed {his} face and someone asked if headquarters was visiting. Apparently being clean needs an explanation.
{name} borrowed a book with three readers already waiting in line. For once, everyone was impatient about something harmless.
A lice inspection interrupted a heated argument about politics. {name} pointed out that at least one enemy had been positively identified.
{name} heard a man laugh on the other side of the enemy parapet. It sounded so ordinary that it was more unsettling than a shot.
{name} tried to remember the sound of the church bell in {home}. Every version sounded like the ration bell.
Part of the parapet collapsed near {name}. Repairs started as soon as the dust settled, with one man on watch while the rest worked.
{name} got a photo of the family house. {He} spent longer looking at the strange curtains than at the faces.
{name} was halfway through a story when {his} listener fell asleep. {He} counted that as a success.
Someone asked {name} to wake them in ten minutes. {He} had no watch, so {he} counted slowly and woke them at what felt like ten.
{name} came off watch and could not say whether the last hour had felt long or short. {He} remembered every move in one patch of wire.
The company barber offered a choice of haircuts. {name} asked to see the second one. The barber laughed.
{name} caught {him}self counting portions before counting people. {He} started again.
The trench wall shook against {name}'s shoulder during the bombardment. {He} pressed both feet into the boards and waited for the next hit.
A story about a goat passed through three dugouts and reached {name} as a story about a general. The ending was the same.
{name} checked the safety catch three times before handing over the post. The man taking over noticed, and checked it once more.
{name} spent the evening teaching a recruit to sew. The recruit pricked a finger and accused the needle of taking sides.
Shellfire stopped the carrying party at a trench junction. {name} waited under a load that got heavier by the minute.
{name} sharpened a pencil carefully and then could not think what to write. {He} put the date at the top anyway.
{name} opened a parcel addressed in unfamiliar handwriting. A note inside said the usual writer had hurt a wrist. {He} read that note first.
{name} traded a cigarette for a pinch of salt. Supper improved. The argument about the exchange rate did not.
A pocket watch went along the bench so everyone could set the time. {name} has no watch, but checked it anyway, just to feel included.
A stretcher party needed the passage. {name} backed into a recess with an ammunition box and stayed there until the last bearer passed.
{name} tried to sketch a horse from memory. The dugout agreed it was a very good dog.
{name} brought sandbags forward and found the damage worse than the message had said. The party went back for another load.
{name} ended a letter with 'nothing to report', then added half a page about the missing soap.
The telephone went dead during the shelling. {name} watched the runner leave with the written orders, then listened for the phone to ring again.
{name} saved a seat for someone fetching supper. Holding it against three hungry men turned out to be hard work.
{name} counted the stitches in a darned sock while waiting for orders. Whoever fixed it had used three colors of wool.
The dugout roof dripped into {name}'s mug. {He} moved the mug. The roof found another way.
{name} stretched a scrap of canvas over the letters. Everything else could get wet first.
Rain washed the chalk names from the trench signs. {name} spent the evening directing strangers past the same junction.
{name} tipped water from a boot and a small beetle climbed out. At least one passenger had enjoyed the crossing.
{name} followed a cough through the fog and found the ration party stuck at a junction. For once, a cough improved supper.
Fog hid the far end of {sector}. {name} kept counting the turns so as not to walk past the dugout.
A familiar voice came out of the fog in the wrong direction. {name} waited for the password before answering.
{name} watched fog gather on the wire until every strand carried beads of water. The sentry beside {him} called it expensive fencing.
{name} warmed the ink bottle inside {his} tunic. The letter began only when the ink agreed to move.
The bread had frozen at the edges. {name} held it near the stove and defended the space with both elbows.
{name} tried to fold a frozen groundsheet. It objected loudly enough to wake the next sleeper.
Frost made each footprint distinct. {name} followed a trail to the missing ration sack and found the quartermaster sitting on it.
{name} aired a blanket in the sunshine and stood beside it, enjoying the same treatment.
The sky stayed clear above {sector}. {name} watched a small cloud form and quietly hoped it would bring friends.
{name} held a letter up to the daylight to read the faint last lines. They were only a shopping list, written on reused paper.
In the clear evening, {name} could see smoke rising far beyond the guns. Somewhere, supper was being cooked in a proper kitchen.
Rain blew in under the dugout door. {name} moved {his} boots out of the wet, then realized they were already inside.
{name} held a loose roof board in place while the storm passed. Every conversation had to wait until {he} could lower both arms.
Thunder shook dust from the beams over {name}. For once, nobody blamed the enemy.
The storm put out the lamp twice. On the third attempt, {name} and two others formed a very irritated windbreak.
Wind kept turning the pages of {name}'s letter. {He} held them down with a biscuit and finished with crumbs in the ink.
{name} spent the afternoon chasing {his} cap across the trench. It stopped every time {he} did, and jumped away again when {he} reached for it.
A loose strip of canvas snapped above {name}'s bunk. {He} tied it down and received thanks from six apparently sleeping men.
The wind carried away the last words of every order. {name} waited until the corporal came closer before picking up anything heavy.
{name} cleaned grit from the rifle bolt with a scrap of cloth. The scrap was once the clean part of a shirt.
The new recruit kept closing both eyes to aim. {name} spent the afternoon helping until one eye stayed open.
{name} checked every ammunition belt by lamplight. One bad cartridge was enough to make {him} start the whole inspection again.
The gun team argued about who carried the heaviest load. {name} offered to swap loads. The argument ended at once.
{name} measured a replacement beam three times in the narrow passage. Nobody wanted to be the one who got it wrong.
A pump handle snapped off in {name}'s hands. {He} fixed it while the water rose around {his} ankles.
A patient apologized for bleeding on {name}'s sleeve. {He} told the patient to concentrate on staying awake.
{name} sorted the dressings by lamplight. When the next stretcher arrived, {he} could find everything without looking.
{name} delivered an urgent message and waited while the officer searched every pocket for a pencil to sign for it.
A new trench junction cost {name} ten minutes. On the way back, {he} marked the right turn with a broken spoon.
{name} noticed a loophole that had been dark for days. {He} watched it until dusk and wrote down what changed.
A beetle crawled across {name}'s sleeve during the long wait. {He} could do nothing about it without giving away the position.
{name} tested the telephone and heard someone at headquarters chewing. The line was declared perfectly clear.
{name} taught a recruit to recognize letters by sound. By supper, the whole table was tapping out Morse on the planks.
{name} counted the ladles in the pot against the men in the queue. The last serving took some careful scraping.
Someone returned an empty pot polished with bread. {name} accepted it as a review.
A man asked {name} to sit nearby without saying anything. {He} stayed until the man fell asleep.
{name} held a service beside a ration store. The men sang quietly so the sleepers behind the wall could rest.
{name} checked the duty roster and noticed the same names on the worst shifts. {He} fetched a fresh sheet of paper and started over.
A report called the trench satisfactory. {name} invited the author to spend a night in it before signing.
{name} lifted the trench periscope and found a spider across the mirror. For one startled second, the enemy seemed enormous.
The listening post reported scraping beyond the wire. {name} waited through an hour of it before a loose stake was found.
A flare caught {name} halfway through a yawn on the fire step. {He} stayed still until {his} jaw ached.
{name} checked the fire step after the shelling. The wall had moved, and the spot where {he} always put {his} foot was gone.
{name} passed ration containers down a chain of hands. By the time supper reached the front, every man smelled of it.
Two carrying parties met in the narrow trench. {name} helped work out how an ammunition box and a very large kettle could pass each other.
{name} stacked spare duckboards beside the junction. Within an hour, the stack had become a bench, a table and an argument.
The relief column arrived early. {name} made room in the shelter by moving everything except the men already asleep.
{name} found a chair in the barn and sat down carefully, as if it might be reserved for someone of higher rank.
The village shop had three kinds of soap. {name} stood at the counter far longer than the purchase required.
{name} watched a woman sweep her doorstep. {He} had forgotten that dirt could be removed permanently from anywhere.
{name} woke up at the usual time for night watch, even in the rear. It took several minutes to convince {him} to go back to sleep.
{name} tried to remember the price of a loaf in {home}. Three different answers seemed right, depending on how far back {he} thought.
A parcel arrived tied with blue ribbon. {name} gave the contents away and kept the ribbon to mark a page.
{name} borrowed a magnifying glass to read cramped handwriting. The urgently needed word turned out to be 'cabbage'.
The section held a competition for the worst joke. {name} won before reaching the end of {his} entry.
{name} was promised a surprise at supper. It was an extra potato. {He} accepted the surprise with proper ceremony.
An old advertisement showed a spotless man smoking beside a fireplace. {name} added a leak above the man's head in pencil.
{name} drew a line on the bench to settle an argument about space. Everyone obeyed it until the broadest man returned from duty.
A child had slipped a riddle into a parcel for {name}. {He} kept the dugout guessing until supper, then turned the page over and read the answer.
{name} took stock of {his} pockets: string, crumbs, a pencil and no sign of the button {he} was looking for.
Someone had used a newspaper to wrap the onions. {name} read a theatre review while peeling supper.
{name} mended a split glove with pale thread. One finger now looks like it has been promoted.
A sneeze blew dust off the shelf above {name}. This caused another sneeze and a discussion about moving the shelf.
{name} has learned to recognize the ration cart by its squeaky wheel. This afternoon, a different squeak caused real disappointment.
The cook borrowed {name}'s mug to measure flour. Getting it back involved waiting for the dough, the baking and the cook's memory.
{name} kept a tally of complaints about the tea. The tally ended when somebody asked whether {he} was volunteering to make it.
A loose thread in {name}'s blanket turned out to be very long. By the time {he} stopped pulling, there was a hole to explain.
{name} read a letter saying the neighbor had married again. The whole dugout wanted the first half of the story, which was missing.
The new soap slipped into the wash bucket. {name} fished it out by feel and then had to wash again.
{name} measured the remaining pencil against the remaining paper. For once, the supplies seemed likely to run out together.
A man asked {name} to describe {home} without mentioning the weather. {He} began with the steepest street and ended with the cheapest lunch.
{name} polished a spoon until {he} could see a small, bent version of {his} face. It looked unimpressed with supper too.
The kettle lid rattled whenever the conversation stopped. {name} put a folded cloth beneath it and immediately missed the noise.
{name} tried to dry a page near the stove. The paper survived, but the message now has the smell of toasted bread.
A scrap of newspaper advertised a sale of garden furniture. {name} worked out how many months of pay a comfortable afternoon would cost.
{name} caught a falling mug with {his} boot. Nobody could say if it was skill or luck, and {he} did not say either.
{name} offered to read the newspaper aloud. The audience asked for the advertisements first, then the racing results, and the war last.
A parcel contained a bar of chocolate broken into uneven pieces. {name} closed {his} eyes while someone else distributed them.
{name} found an old shopping list inside a coat pocket. Soap, lamp oil, apples. {He} folded it along the original creases.
{name} laughed at something nobody else had heard. Asked to share it, {he} admitted remembering a conversation from years ago.
A borrowed towel came back cleaner than when {name} lent it. {He} is considering lending out the rest of the washing.
{name} tried to write neatly for the first line of a letter. By the third, {he} was writing as quickly as the thoughts arrived.
The last of the jam was shared by [passing the tin around|scraping it onto a biscuit|adding hot water and calling it a drink]. {name} approved the method.
{name} put [a flat stone|an empty tin|a folded ration label] under a short table leg. Supper stopped sliding toward the corporal.
{name} offered [a biscuit|a length of string|a spare button] for a better place near the stove. The offer was refused with surprising dignity.
{name} cleaned the rifle for the third time today. The sergeant said it was already clean. {name} said it could be cleaner.
{name} counted the rounds in the pouch twice and got two different numbers. {He} decided the second one was the right one.
{name} spent the afternoon fixing a loose sling with a piece of telephone wire. It held. {He} was prouder of that than of any shot.
A new recruit asked {name} how to hold a rifle in the cold. {name} showed the boy, then showed him again, slower.
{name} carved a notch in the stock for every day on the line. There is not much wood left.
{name} wrapped the rifle bolt in a rag to keep the dirt out. The rag was a sock. The sock was not {his}.
{name} traded half a ration of tobacco for a better rifle oil. The deal was fair, and nobody else would have made it.
The squad lined up to have their rifles looked over. {name}'s was the only one the officer did not hand back with a frown.
{name} practiced loading with {his} eyes shut. After an hour, {he} could do it in the time it takes to cough.
{name} found a bullet on the trench floor, still shiny. {He} put it in {his} pocket for luck, then took it out again, just in case.
{name} was ordered to fire only on a clear target. {He} waited all day for one. It was the longest day of the week.
{name} sewed a torn coat before sewing a torn man. The man did not mind. He was asleep.
{name} was handed a boot full of water and a man with a hole in his foot. {He} dealt with both.
A boy asked {name} if it would hurt. {name} said yes, and then talked about the sea until it was over.
{name} ran out of clean bandages at noon and boiled the old ones in a mess tin. They were whiter than before.
{name} checked every man in the section for lice. It took two hours. The squad called it the most thorough inspection of the war.
A man with a cough would not report to the aid post. {name} walked up to {sector} and listened to the man's chest on the fire step.
{name} tied a splint with a bayonet scabbard and a bootlace. It looked terrible and worked perfectly.
{name} found a patient asleep on a stretcher and stood guard over the stretcher until the surgeon came.
Three men came in with the same blisters. {name} gave them the same advice: change your socks, and then change them again.
{name} put a red cross on a clean white sheet and hung it outside the aid post. It was the only color for miles.
{name} wrote every patient's name on a card and pinned it to the stretcher. By dawn, the whole row looked like a small school.
{name} was thanked by a man who could not remember {his} name. {name} said that was fine. They never do.
{name} stirred the pot and tasted it. {He} added salt, then pepper, then a long silence. The silence helped the most.
{name} baked flat bread on a shovel over the fire. It was the first bread that tasted like bread in a month.
{name} found a sack of onions behind a ruined barn. The squad ate onion soup for three days and wept happily.
The queue for soup was long. {name} gave the last man a double portion without being asked.
{name} boiled coffee in a bucket and strained it through a sock. Nobody asked which sock.
{name} carried the stew up to {sector} in two pails. A shell burst nearby. The soup survived. The carrier shook, but the soup did not spill.
{name} was given a goose by a farmer who would not say where it came from. The goose was cooked within the hour. Nobody asked a single question.
{name} made a pie out of bully beef and old biscuits. It was ugly, and the squad scraped the dish clean.
{name} chopped wood for the stove until dark. The stove was warm, the soup was hot, and {he} was the only one who did not sit down.
The ration truck was late, so {name} made soup from the last of everything. It was thin, but it was hot.
{name} gave a new recruit a wooden spoon with a small carving on the handle. 'So you do not lose it,' {he} said.
{name} washed the pots by lamplight and sang under {his} breath. Half the dugout fell asleep to it.
{name} spent the night repairing a telephone line cut by a shell. {He} found the break at dawn, a yard from where {he} started.
{name} sent a message with a lamp from {sector}: three long, two short, a pause. The answer came back: understood.
{name} tested the field telephone and heard a stranger humming on the line. {He} hummed back. The line went quiet.
{name} wound a spool of wire across a shelled road at night. By morning the line was working, and the road was not.
{name} taught the runner a simple code of knocks on a board. By evening the whole dugout was knocking back.
{name} was asked for a message to the colonel. It took a minute to send and four hours to be answered.
A bird nested in the telephone box at {sector}. {name} refused to move it until the eggs hatched.
{name} listened to the line all night. {He} heard the war breathing in it, far away, and then silence.
The telephone rang once at three in the morning. {name} answered. It was the wrong number. {name} stayed up anyway.
{name} repaired the field telephone with a button, a bent nail and a piece of chewing gum. It worked until noon.
{name} climbed a pole at {sector} to fix the line. Halfway up, {he} remembered {he} did not like heights. {He} finished the job anyway.
{name} tested every flag signal twice before sending it. A wrong message is worse than a late one.
{name} shored up a collapsing wall at {sector} with planks from an old door. It held. It still had a number on it.
{name} spent the night digging a drain in the trench floor. By morning, the water was running the right way.
{name} checked the wire at {sector} with gloves on and a lantern off. {He} found two gaps and closed them.
{name} rolled out a coil of barbed wire in the dark. A thorn caught {his} sleeve, and {he} said exactly one word.
{name} cut firewood from a broken fence. The fence was the only thing between the squad and a field of mud.
{name} measured the depth of a new trench with a stick and a piece of string. It was two inches short. The squad dug two more.
{name} built a rack for rifles out of ammunition boxes. The corporal inspected it and said it was too neat.
{name} reinforced a dugout roof with logs and sandbags. It will not stop a big shell, but it will stop the dust.
{name} laid duckboards in {sector}. The first man to walk on them said it was like a street in a real town.
{name} dug a small ditch around the aid post to carry water away. The medic thanked {him} with a boiled egg.
{name} found a crack in the parapet at {sector} and filled it with sandbags and stones. The next bullet hit the stones and did no harm.
{name} sharpened a shovel until it could shave. {He} did not shave with it, but the squad respected the shovel.
{name} ran a message from {sector} to the colonel's dugout and back in twenty minutes. It was a record, and nobody timed it.
{name} carried a bag of mail through a shelled trench. Every letter arrived. Two had mud on them.
{name} learned the shortest way between three dugouts and a bad corner. {He} drew it on a boot sole with chalk.
A message was too important to write down. {name} memorized it and repeated it under {his} breath all the way to the front line.
{name} crossed the open ground between {sector} and the support trench in six seconds. Nobody saw {him}, which is the idea.
{name} was handed a note with no address. {He} asked around for an hour and delivered it to a man who cried.
{name} had a message for the lieutenant and found only the lieutenant's cap. The lieutenant was in the next trench. The message was delivered, late.
{name} slept three hours between runs and woke up already running. {His} legs did not have an opinion.
A shell burst behind {name} halfway to {sector}. {He} did not look back, and arrived with the message and a ringing head.
{name} carried two pails of water and a message at the same time. The water arrived first.
{name} was thanked by an officer, which is rare. {He} wrote it in {his} notebook so nobody could say it did not happen.
{name} waited in a dugout doorway for a gap in the firing. It came after ten minutes. {He} went through it like a rabbit.
{name} spent six hours in a hole at {sector} watching a single gap in the enemy wire. Nothing moved. It was a good day.
{name} lay still while a rat ran across {his} back. It took all the self-control {he} owned.
{name} cleaned the scope with a corner of a handkerchief. It is the cleanest thing in the trench.
{name} made a hat out of grass and burlap and wore it for the whole shift. Even the squad could not find {him}.
{name} watched a bird land on the enemy parapet and stay a full minute. {He} had a clear shot and did not take it.
{name} measured the distance to a lone post in the open and wrote it down. The number was 412. {He} circled it twice.
{name} took one shot in the whole day. It was the only one needed.
{name} climbed out before dawn and crawled to a new position. Behind a stump, in the dark, {he} waited for the light.
{name} was told not to fire until the order came. The order did not come. {He} lay still for eight hours anyway.
{name} swapped places with a spotter and found out how hard the job really is. The spotter bought {him} a mug of tea after.
{name} slept in the afternoon so as not to sleep in the dark. It is the strangest schedule on the front.
{name} drew the enemy line from memory in a notebook. Every sandbag, every post. The officers asked to borrow it.
{name} cleaned every part of the machine gun with an old toothbrush. The gun was happier, and so was the crew.
{name} oiled the gun until it shone. A man leaned on it and left a fingerprint. {name} cleaned it again, without a word.
{name} carried the heavy tripod up the trench on {his} shoulders, swearing quietly in two languages.
{name} counted the belts in the box and found one missing. {He} searched the whole position and found it under the cook's coat.
The machine gun jammed at {sector}. {name} fixed it in the dark with a pocketknife and a lot of patience.
{name} tested the gun with a short burst. The enemy answered with silence. {He} counted that as a draw.
{name} taught the new loader how to feed the belt. It took six tries, two curses and a spoon.
{name} built a roof of boards over the gun position. The crew sleeps under it and calls it the hotel.
{name} was ordered to hold fire until the signal. {He} waited with a finger on the trigger and a sweat on {his} neck.
{name} swapped the barrel with a cool one and left the hot one in a bucket of water. The bucket hissed for a minute.
{name} dragged the gun to a new position at {sector} before dawn. It weighs a good deal more at four in the morning.
{name} fell asleep behind the gun. The loader covered {him} with a blanket and took the watch.
{name} walked the whole trench at {sector} before dawn, shaking every hand. It took an hour and made a small difference.
{name} read the orders three times and kept the important one for the squad. The others went in the stove.
{name} gave up a seat in the dugout to a wounded man and spent the night on a box. The squad noticed.
{name} drew a map of the sector on the back of a ration crate. By the end of the day, three officers had copied it.
{name} inspected the rifles and found them clean. {He} inspected them again to be sure. They were still clean.
{name} wrote letters for six men who could not write. It took the whole evening and a pencil.
{name} was asked by the colonel how morale was. {He} said it was good, and then told the truth after the colonel left.
{name} stayed on the fire step for two hours so the sentries could eat. Nobody had asked {him}.
{name} praised a private by name in front of the whole line. The private went red and stood a little taller for a week.
{name} got a new pair of boots from the quartermaster and gave them to the man with the worst feet.
{name} shared a plan with the squad before the patrol. Every man could repeat it. That is the whole of command.
{name} stood at the door of the dugout and told every man that came in: well done today. Most of them did not know what for.
{name} held a service in a dugout with a ration box for an altar. The congregation was twelve men and a dog.
{name} wrote a letter home for a man who could not find the words. It took an hour and the man dictated one sentence.
{name} sat with a frightened recruit through the night and said very little. By morning, the boy was sleeping.
{name} blessed the bread before the meal, and the soup after. The cook considered it part of the recipe.
{name} walked along the line at dusk with a lantern. Every man {he} passed nodded. Some bowed their heads.
{name} said a prayer for the dead in a language half the squad did not know. They stood anyway.
{name} listened to a corporal talk for an hour about his farm. {He} nodded in the right places and did not interrupt.
{name} shared a pouch of tobacco with a man who had not spoken for two days. By the end of the pipe, the man said thank you.
{name} made a small cross from two rifle cleaning rods and a piece of wire. It hangs above the aid post door.
{name} read a psalm aloud at {sector} while the guns were quiet. It was the only quiet hour of the week.
{name} carried water to the wounded along the stretcher row. {He} said nothing, only gave each man a cup and moved on.
{name} walked to the graves behind the line with a bucket and a brush, and cleaned each cross by hand.
{name} found a clean spoon in the trench and kept it. It was the best find of the week.
{name} spent the morning shaving with a cracked mirror and cold water. The result looked like a map of a small country.
{name} wrote a short letter home. The first line said: I am well. The second line said: really.
A mouse ran across {name}'s boot and into a biscuit tin. {He} let it stay. It was the only visitor all day.
{name} traded a button for a pinch of tea. By the end of the week, the button had come back, and so had the tea.
{name} learned a new card game from a man in the next trench. {He} lost, and was told it was a good start.
A quiet afternoon. {name} sat on an ammunition box and watched the smoke from the stove make shapes.
{name} tried to sleep and could not. {He} counted sandbags until the count came out odd, and then started again.
{name} helped dig a latrine and later dug a second one in a better spot. The first was relabeled as a storage pit.
{name} found a bent fork in the mud and polished it for an hour. {He} now owns the best fork in the squad.
{name} listened to a corporal tell the same story for the fourth time. The ending changed again.
{name} mended a hole in {his} sock with a piece of {his} shirt. The squad called it a new uniform.
{name} was given a pencil and a scrap of paper and wrote a poem. It had six lines and one rhyme. The squad cheered the rhyme.
{name} borrowed a razor and returned it cleaner than before. It was the first compliment the owner had had in weeks.
{name} spent a quiet hour looking at a photograph and not saying whose it was.
The squad played a game of guessing what was in the stew. {name} was the closest and nobody wanted to know.
{name} found a pair of dry socks and put them on. For a whole minute, nothing in the war mattered.
{name} was woken by a rat on the chest and let it be. They shared the dugout and agreed on nothing.
{name} read the same page of an old newspaper five times. It was the only reading material within a mile.
{name} tried to whistle a tune and found that {he} had forgotten the second half. {He} hummed the first half all day.
{name} drew a face on a tin cup with a charred stick. The cup has been watching over the dugout ever since.
A cheerful man from the next unit came by to borrow a match. {name} gave {him} the whole box and regretted nothing.
{name} was made to clean the mess tins. {He} did it carefully and with great ceremony, to make a point.
{name} watched the sun rise from the fire step and thought of nothing. It was the best part of the day.
{name} traded stories with a man from the far side of the country. Neither could understand the other's accent, and neither minded.
{name} found a tiny flower growing in a crack in the sandbags. {He} told nobody and watered it from {his} canteen.
{name} was woken at midnight for a false alarm. {He} went back to bed and dreamed of a real one.
{name} sorted the squad's letters by size and then by smell. The mail sergeant was not amused.
{name} left a note on the dugout wall: 'Back soon.' Somebody added: 'Sure.' Somebody else added: 'We hope.'
{name} swapped boots with a man whose feet were the same size and whose luck was better. Time will tell.
{name} spent the night on the fire step at {sector}, watching a dark line that might have been a hedge.
Two flares went up over {place}. {name} counted the seconds between them and the sound. It was a habit by now.
{name} heard a shovel in the dark beyond the wire. {He} reported it to the sergeant, who nodded and said: ours or theirs?
At {sector}, {name} spent an hour looking at the same patch of ground. By dawn, {he} knew every stone.
{name} was woken by a sentry shaking {his} boot. The sentry had nothing to say. He only wanted company.
{name} peeked through a loophole and saw a rabbit between the lines. For a moment, nobody fired.
{name} cleaned the loophole at {sector} with a stick. It had filled with dirt from last night's bursts.
{name} took the middle watch and stared at the wire. A cloud passed over the moon, and the wire seemed to walk.
A sudden burst of firing woke the line. {name} grabbed {his} rifle and jumped onto the fire step, then found nothing. It was a false alarm.
{name} replaced a torn sandbag at {sector} with a new one. A small job. The squad noticed and said nothing, which is a thank you.
{name} checked the wire at {sector} on {his} hands and knees. It was whole. {He} returned before dawn with mud on {his} chin.
{name} watched a patrol leave the trench at {sector} and counted them out. Later {he} counted them in.
{name} was ordered to hold the loophole until relief. It came four hours late. {He} did not complain.
A flare hung over {place} for a long time. {name} saw the whole of no man's land at once, and did not forget it.
{name} drank cold tea from a mess tin on the fire step. It was terrible, and it was the best part of the watch.
{name} carried a load of sandbags up the communication trench. The trench is long, and {his} back is longer.
{name} cut wood for the stove at the support dugout. The stack is higher than the dugout.
{name} repaired a broken ladder at {sector} with two nails and a good deal of language.
{name} was sent to fetch water from a well behind the line. It took three trips and a lot of care.
{name} unpacked a crate of tins and counted them twice. There were eleven. The list said twelve.
{name} spent the day digging a new communication trench. By dusk, it was almost a trench.
{name} helped haul an ammunition box up the slope. The box was heavy. So was the silence.
{name} swept the dugout floor with a branch. The floor did not improve, but the dugout smelled of pine.
{name} sorted the ammunition by caliber and then by mood. The cases were in better humor than the men.
{name} was given a mallet and told to drive twenty stakes. By nightfall, {he} had driven nineteen and a thumb.
{name} guarded a store of rations against rats for the whole shift. The rats won on points.
{name} was handed a lantern and a map and told to find a supply dump that had moved. It had. {He} found it anyway.
In reserve, {name} washed a shirt in a bucket and hung it on a rifle to dry. It looked like a flag of surrender.
{name} slept in a barn with fifty others. The snoring formed a kind of music, and {he} fell asleep to it.
{name} got a day of rest and spent it sitting on a wall. Nothing happened, and it was lovely.
{name} walked into the village and bought an apple. It was the best apple of {his} life, and {he} told everyone.
{name} had a hot bath in a big tub with three other men. The water was gray. The mood was golden.
{name} was given a new pair of boots. They did not fit, and {he} cherished them anyway.
{name} played cards in the hayloft with a deck missing the queen of hearts. The game was fairer without her.
{name} wrote a long letter home. It said very little and ran to four pages.
{name} was detailed to paint the sergeant's name on a board. {He} got the spelling right on the second try.
{name} sat in the sun and watched the horses graze. They did not seem to know there was a war.
{name} was inspected, drilled and fed in that order. {He} liked the last part best.
{name} listened to a band play in the square. The tuba was a little flat, and the crowd did not care.

promotion: For keeping {his} head when others lost theirs at {place}, {name} was promoted to {rank}.
The old {oldRank} did not come back from the wire. {name} wears {his} stripes now: {rank}.
{name} brought back a wounded man and a lost machine gun from {place} in one trip. {He} is {rank} now.
Nobody else in {sector} wanted the stripes. {name} said yes. {rank}.
The colonel asked who held the line at {place} last night. Every finger pointed at {name}. {rank}.
{name} was made {rank}. {He} celebrated by sleeping four hours in a row.
{name} was promoted to {rank}. The first request addressed to the new rank concerned a blocked drain.
The order named {name} as {rank}. {He} read it twice, then asked who would take over {his} watch.
{name} received the rank of {rank} and a stack of unfinished paperwork. The congratulations lasted less time than the paperwork.
Promoted to {rank}, {name} had to settle an argument {he} had been happily taking part in five minutes earlier.
{name} is {rank} now. At supper, a recruit waited for {him} to sit before taking a place. {He} noticed.
The promotion to {rank} reached {name} on a creased slip of paper. {He} smoothed it and put it with the letters from home.
{name} was made {rank} after keeping the section together under fire. {He} asked that the rest of the section be mentioned too.
{name} accepted promotion to {rank}. Later, {he} practised giving the morning orders quietly enough not to wake the dugout.
{name} has been made {rank}. The new stripes were sewn on by a man who admitted he had never sewn anything before.
The sergeant read out the order at {sector}: {name} is now {rank}. The squad cheered, and the new {rank} asked for quiet.
{name} was promoted to {rank} after bringing a message through a barrage at {place}. {He} says the message was not important. It was.
{name} took charge of the squad at {sector} when the {oldRank} fell. By morning, the squad had a new {rank}.
{name} is {rank} now. The stripes are crooked, and {he} refuses to straighten them.
{name} got the stripe of {rank} for steady nerves at {place}. The squad has not decided if it is a gift or a punishment.
wounded: Shrapnel at {place}. {name} walked to the aid post on {his} own feet and asked for a cigarette before the stitches.
{name} was caught by gas at {sector}. {He} coughs in {his} sleep but swears {he} will be back on the line within the week.
A rifle grenade burst above {sector}. {name} took a splinter in the arm and refused to leave until the next man was bandaged.
{name} was buried by a shell at {place}. They dug {him} out after twenty minutes, deaf in one ear and still holding {item}.
Trench foot. {name} can no longer feel {his} toes and the medical officer has ordered {him} to the rear, swearing at the mud.
{name} was hit by a sniper at {place}. The bullet went through {his} shoulder and, somehow, missed everything that mattered.
A fever swept through {sector}. {name} was carried out shaking and talking to people who were not there.
Barbed wire at {place} opened {name}'s leg from knee to ankle. {He} limped back in carrying the wire-cutters, as ordered.
A splinter caught {name} at {sector}. At the aid post, {he} was more upset about the ruined sleeve than the dressing beneath it.
{name} reached the aid post with a wounded hand held against {his} chest. Someone else had to unfasten the buttons.
Flying masonry struck {name} at {place}. The stretcher jolted over every familiar board on the way out.
{name} took a bullet in the leg at {sector}. {He} passed the rifle to the next man before allowing the bearers to lift {him}.
The blast at {place} threw {name} against the trench wall. At the aid post, the questions sounded far away.
{name} was wounded during shelling at {sector}. The last thing {he} asked before leaving was whether the relief had arrived.
A fragment struck {name}'s shoulder. The dressing covered a pocket {he} kept trying to reach, until an orderly retrieved its contents.
{name} was carried from {place} with a wounded leg. {He} apologised whenever the bearers had to stop.
{name} was hit at {place}. The medic bandaged {him} where {he} fell and then looked around for the next man.
Something burned across {name}'s shoulder at {sector}. {He} did not feel the pain until the squad pointed at the blood.
{name} took a splinter in the thigh at {place}. {He} limped to the aid post and refused help the whole way.
A piece of metal hit {name} at {place}. It was small, but it was deep, and the medic's face said so.
{name} was caught in the open at {sector}. {He} crawled the last ten yards to the trench on {his} elbows.
At {place} {name} was hit and fell without a sound. The man beside {him} thought {he} was joking until the blood showed.
A hot splinter went into {name}'s arm at {sector}. {He} pulled it out and found it was still warm.
{name} was wounded at {place}. {He} asked only one thing: that someone send {his} watch home if it came to that.
recovered: {name} is back from the field hospital, thinner and quieter, with {item} still in {his} pocket.
{name} came back to {sector} with a new scar and an old joke. The squad was glad of both.
The field hospital let {name} go. {He} came back up the line on foot because the truck would not wait.
{name} returned from hospital carrying letters, chocolate and rumours, and handed out all three.
Back with {his} platoon, {name} found that someone had kept {his} place on the fire step. Nobody admitted who.
{name} returned from hospital and found a new face beside the bunk. The old argument about shelf space resumed immediately.
Declared fit, {name} reported back to {sector}. The familiar smell reached {him} before the familiar voices.
{name} came back from hospital with a clean shirt. The men admired it from a respectful distance.
The medical officer cleared {name} for duty. At {sector}, someone quietly moved a pack off {his} usual seat.
{name} returned with instructions to take care. The corporal read them, looked around {sector}, and folded them carefully.
Back from hospital, {name} distributed messages from other recovering men. For an hour, the dugout sounded like a railway waiting room.
{name} rejoined {sector} carrying a borrowed book from the ward. It is now overdue, which {he} says is a good reason to stay alive.
{name} came back fit for duty and discovered the section had changed the recipe for its tea. {He} demanded an explanation.
{name} left the aid post this morning with a limp and a sack of bandages. {He} reached {sector} by noon.
{name} is back on the line at {sector}. The squad found {him} a dry place and a hot cup.
{name} came back from the hospital thinner than before, with a new scar and a short beard. {He} fell asleep on the fire step in an hour.
{name} is well again. {He} hung {his} bandages on a nail at {sector} like medals.
When {name} returned to {sector}, the squad had kept {his} spot. {He} thanked them with the last of {his} tobacco.
{name} walked back up the communication trench to {sector}, slowly, looking at everything as if for the first time.
{name} spent the first night back at {sector} not sleeping. {He} said the quiet was too loud.
{name} was welcomed back to {sector} with a handshake from every man in the squad. It took a while.
fallen: {name} fell at {place}. They found {item} in {his} pocket and sent it home with a letter that said {he} was brave. It was true.
The wire at {place} took {name}. {His} friends in {sector} carved {his} name into a duckboard so the mud would remember {him}.
{name} went over the top at {place} and did not come back. The roll was called twice. Nobody answered for {him}.
A shell found {name} in the dugout at {sector}. The men put {his} helmet on a cross by the road. It is still there.
{name} died at the aid post at dawn, holding {item}. The chaplain says {he} was smiling. The chaplain says that about everyone, but this time it was true.
{name} was lost in the mine explosion under {place}. There was nothing to bury. They buried {his} name instead.
{name} was killed at {place}. At supper, someone began to set out another mug, then put it back.
A shell killed {name} at {sector}. The letter in {his} kit was finished except for the signature.
{name} fell during the fighting at {place}. The corporal checked the spelling before sending the report.
{name} died at the aid post. An orderly recorded {his} name, gathered the personal effects and sat still for a moment before the next stretcher.
{name} was killed at {sector}. A small debt owed to {him} was written off without discussion.
The fighting at {place} claimed {name}. Nobody wanted the space on the shelf, though everyone had wanted it yesterday.
{name} did not survive the bombardment. The section collected the letters from {his} pack and tied them with their original string.
{name} fell at {place}. A man who barely knew {him} remembered being lent a needle and asked to help write home.
heir: {name} came to the front because {his} {relation} {prevName} never came home. {He} carries {item}.
The papers say {name}. The sergeant says {he} has {his} {relation}'s eyes. {prevName}'s eyes. Nobody in {sector} argues.
A letter came with {name}: "I am {prevName}'s {relation}. I have come to finish what {he} started." Nobody had the heart to tell {him} it never finishes.
{name} took the same post at {sector} where {prevName} stood. {He} found {his} {relation}'s initials carved in the wall and put {his} own beneath them.
The House of {family} sent another. {name}, {relation} of {prevName}, arrived with the same eyes and the same stubborn silence.
{name} arrived carrying the family name of {prevName}. The corporal asked how to pronounce {his} first name, and waited for the answer.
The House of {family} sent {name} after {prevName}. This time the family packed two pairs of spare socks.
{name} asked about {prevName} on arriving at {sector}. The first story concerned a stolen breakfast. {He} asked for another.
{name} put {item} beside the bunk. Someone who had known {prevName} helped clear the shelf without saying why.
{name} had heard about {prevName}'s courage. At {sector}, {he} also heard about the snoring, the cards and the terrible handwriting.
The papers connected {name} to {prevName}. The men took longer to learn {name}'s own habits, but they made the effort.
{name} joined {sector} under the shadow of {prevName}'s name. At the first roll call, the corporal used the right one.
Another member of the House of {family} reached the line: {name}. {He} asked where {prevName} had slept, then chose a different corner.
missing: {name} went out with a patrol to {place} and did not come back with it. {He} is listed as missing. The men leave {his} rations untouched.
After the raid on {place}, {name} was not at the roll call. Somebody saw {him} in a shell hole. Somebody else says that was someone else.
{name} took a message across {place} at dusk. The message arrived. {name} did not.
{name} was absent when the patrol returned from {place}. The corporal checked the list against the faces, then checked it again.
The last report placed {name} near {place}. By evening, no later report had arrived. Missing.
After the shelling at {sector}, nobody could account for {name}. {His} kit remains beside the bunk.
{name} failed to return from the wire. A search found tracks leading into churned ground and nothing certain beyond it.
At roll call, {name}'s place stayed empty. Someone said another section might have taken {him} in. A runner was sent to ask.
The party came back from {place} by different routes. By dawn, everyone had been accounted for except {name}.
{name} was last seen moving toward cover at {place}. No one agrees which shelter. The report lists {him} as missing.
The relief reached {sector} without {name}. {His} name was added to a list the corporal kept separate from the dead.
returned: {name} crawled back into {sector} at dawn after two nights in a shell hole at {place}, covered in mud and carrying {item}. {He} asked if {he} had missed breakfast.
The sentry nearly shot {name} coming in through the wire. {He} had been lost near {place} for two days, living on puddle water and stubbornness.
{name} turned up at a neighbouring battalion, having walked the wrong way for a day and a half. {He} came home to {sector} with three new friends and no explanation.
{name} came back to {sector} after sheltering with another unit. {He} brought a note confirming the story and a borrowed mug to return.
The missing report was still on the desk when {name} walked in. The clerk crossed it out hard enough to tear the paper.
{name} returned after being cut off near {place}. {He} knew the password, but could barely make the sentry hear it.
Found with a party from another section, {name} was guided back to {sector}. The relief on the corporal's face lasted until the lecture began.
{name} returned by a trench nobody thought passable. {He} asked for water before explaining how little of it was still a trench.
A sentry called down that {name} was at the wire. Three men went to help before anyone gave an order.
{name} reappeared at {sector} carrying a scrap of map from another unit. The route home had been drawn over somebody's shopping list.
{name} came back exhausted, having waited in cover until the way cleared. {He} slept through the argument about who had worried most.
comrade: {a} and {b} split the last tin of beef, counting the bites out loud to keep it fair.
{a} kept watch so that {b} could sleep. Then {bs} kept watch so that {as} could. Neither slept.
{a} taught {b} to play the harmonica. The whole squad has asked them both, politely, to stop.
{a} pulled {b} out of a flooded shell hole at {place}. Neither has mentioned it since. Both remember.
{a} and {b} argued all night about whose hometown has the better beer. They agreed to finish the argument after the war.
{a} cut {b}'s hair with a bayonet and a cracked mirror. It is not good. It is, however, short.
{a} wrote a letter for {b}'s mother, because {bs} could not find the words. {bs} signed it.
{a} and {b} carved a chessboard into an ammunition box. The pieces are bullets, buttons and one very patient beetle.
{a} and {b} made a pact on sentry tonight: whoever gets home first visits the other's family. They shook on it.
{a} saw {b} freeze up on the fire step at {place}. {as} said nothing, just stood closer. It was enough.
{a} and {b} divided a parcel using a tin lid as scales. The last crumb needed a second opinion.
{a} held the mirror while {b} shaved. The arrangement survived the shaving but not the comments.
{a} and {b} compared drawings of home. Both drawings included a kitchen table larger than the house.
{a} lent {b} a pencil. It came back wrapped in a scrap of paper that said 'One good turn'.
{a} and {b} carried a kettle through three narrow turns without spilling a drop. The applause at the end caused the accident.
{a} fixed the strap on {b}'s pack. The price was a biscuit and a promise to stop mentioning the haircut.
{a} and {b} tried to invent a new card game. The rules only made sense once they stopped betting tobacco.
{a} and {b} sat through a quiet hour without finding anything to say. At the change of watch, the next pair was told it had been a good hour.
{a} lost a boot in the trench. {b} found it, stuffed it with dry socks, and gave it back without a word.
{a} and {b} carved a chess set out of candle wax. The kings melted too close to the stove, so the game goes on without them.
{a} reads {b}'s letters from home out loud, because {bs} never learned to read. {as} leaves out the sad parts. {bs} knows.
{a} and {b} share one pair of good gloves on watch, one glove each. It is not practical. It is friendship.
{a} snores. {b} does not. {bs} now sleeps with a sock stuffed in each ear, and the two are still friends.
{a} owes {b} so many cigarettes that they stopped counting and started writing it down. The notebook is nearly full.
{a} wrote a song about {place}. {b} wrote a second verse. The squad has banned the third.
{a} and {b} found a cat in the ruins at {place} and argued for an hour about its name. The cat settled it by sleeping on {bs}.
{a} mended the hole in {b}'s trousers with fishing line and a bent pin. {bs} says the patch is stronger than the trousers.
{a} kept {b} awake all night with questions about home: the street, the shop, the dog. By morning {as} could have walked there blind.
{a} and {b} made a pact: whoever gets home first visits the other's mother. They shook on it twice, to be sure.
{a} gave {b} the last match in the trench. {bs} used it to light a candle so that {as} could finish a letter.
{a} and {b} spent an hour hunting rats with a bucket and a piece of cheese. Score at dusk: rats 4, soldiers 1.
{b} fell asleep on watch. {a} took over without waking {bs}, and told the sergeant nothing.
{a} taught {b} three words in the language of home. {bs} uses all three at the wrong moment, every day.
{a} and {b} cooked a stew from everything in their pockets: one onion, two biscuits and a button. They ate all of it except the button.
{a} lent {b} a razor. It came back sharper, with a new handle carved from an old tent peg.
{a} and {b} have a secret signal: two taps on the helmet means 'still here'. They use it every night after the flares go out.
{a} drew a map of {b}'s hometown from {bs}'s stories. {bs} says it is wrong in every detail, and carries it everywhere.
{a} carried {b}'s rifle all the way up to {place} after {bs} twisted an ankle. Neither has said thank you. Neither needs to.
{a} and {b} both swear they saw a ghost at {place}. Each says the other screamed first.
{a} saved the last of the sugar for {b}'s birthday. Nobody knows if it really was {bs}'s birthday. It was a good day anyway.
{a} lent {b} a spare pair of socks. {b} promised to return them. Both knew that would not happen.
{a} and {b} found a puddle of dry ground and fought over it for an hour. They ended up sharing it.
{a} caught {b} writing a love letter and read it over {bs} shoulder. {b} threw a boot. {a} told nobody.
{a} saved {b}'s last cigarette from a falling sandbag. {b} did not say thanks, but kept the stub.
{b} taught {a} how to tie a perfect knot. {a} used it to tie {as} boots together by mistake.
{a} and {b} sat back to back all night to keep warm, and agreed not to mention it in the morning.
{a} carried {b}'s pack for half a mile and never said a word. {b} noticed.
{a} and {b} swapped hats for a day to see if anyone would notice. Nobody did, and both were a little insulted.
{a} read a page of {b}'s diary by accident. {a} did not tell, but was kinder for a week.
{b} woke {a} from a nightmare by calling {as} name. {a} did not say thank you, but poured the tea.
{a} and {b} made a pact: whoever got leave first would visit the other's mother. They shook on it.
{a} found a blister on {b}'s heel and bound it with a strip of {as} own shirt. {b} did not argue.
{a} and {b} tried to teach the squad a song in two languages. The squad learned the wrong half of each.
{a} and {b} disagreed about the best way to make tea. The tea was ruined, and so was the afternoon.
{a} gave {b} the dry end of the bunk and took the wet one. {b} noticed and said, quietly, that they would swap tomorrow.
{a} and {b} stood watch together and traded jokes in whispers. The jokes were old, but the whispers were new.
{a} found {b}'s lost photo in the mud and wiped it clean before returning it. Neither mentioned it again.
{a} and {b} built a small shelf out of a cracker box. It holds two mugs, a candle and one shared hope.
{a} fell asleep on {b}'s shoulder during a rest. {b} sat very still for an hour.
{a} ate {b}'s portion by mistake and spent the rest of the day apologizing in tobacco.
enemy: At {place}, {a} of the {af} and {b} of the {bf} traded insults across the wire for an hour. By the end they were trading recipes.
{a} ({af}) and {b} ({bf}) ended up in the same shell hole at {place}. They stared at each other. Then each crawled home, and neither has told anyone.
{b} of the {bf} threw a tin of tobacco into the {af} trench with a note: "for the one who sings". {a} kept the tin.
{a} had {b} of the {bf} in the sights at {place} for a long second. {b} was lighting a pipe. {a} let the match burn all the way down.
A football came over the parapet from the {bf} side with {b}'s name scratched on it. {a} kicked it back. It did not come again.
On a quiet night {a} ({af}) and {b} ({bf}) called out their names across no man's land, just to hear another voice. Now each knows exactly who is out there.
At {place}, {a} of the {af} and {b} of the {bf} spent the morning shooting at the same loose sheet of metal. The sheet kept winning.
{a} ({af}) and {b} ({bf}) spotted the same abandoned cart near {place}. A long exchange of shots left the cart exactly where it was.
During a lull at {place}, {a} called across from the {af} line. {b} answered from the {bf} side with a perfect imitation of an officer. Both trenches went quiet.
{a} of the {af} and {b} of the {bf} watched a broken branch near {place} all morning. Neither could risk assuming it was only a branch.
{a} ({af}) shouted a challenge across to {b} ({bf}) at {place}. The answer was lost under the guns. Nobody repeated the challenge.
At {place}, {a} and {b} exchanged rifle shots until a shell burst between the positions. For a while, both rifles remained silent.
{a} of the {af} spotted {b} of the {bf} repairing a parapet at {place}. A warning shot stopped the repair on the spot.
A bucket appeared above the {bf} parapet at {place}. {a} fired. {b} pulled the bucket down. Later a sign went up: 'Water costs enough already.'
{b} of the {bf} shouted a joke across the wire at {place}. {a} of the {af} laughed before remembering not to. Both lines heard it.
{a} ({af}) and {b} ({bf}) came to the same broken well at {place} at night, each with a bucket. They filled them in turns and backed away.
{b} of the {bf} lost a cap on a night patrol near {place}. {a} of the {af} found it in the morning and now wears it on Sundays.
{a} of the {af} and {b} of the {bf} have been shooting at the same tin can on the wire at {place} for a week. Both trenches keep score.
A note came over the wire at {place}, wrapped around a stone: 'Stop singing, {af}. Signed, {b}.' {a} sang louder.
{a} ({af}) watched {b} ({bf}) drag a wounded man back across no man's land at {place}, and held fire until both were gone.
{a} of the {af} and {b} of the {bf} have carved their names into the same post in no man's land at {place}. It is getting crowded.
Across the wire at {place}, {b} of the {bf} held up a sign: 'How is your coffee?' {a} of the {af} held up a sign back: 'Worse than yours.'
{a} ({af}) threw a loaf of bread into the {bf} trench at {place}. An hour later a sausage came back with a note from {b}: 'Fair trade.'
{a} of the {af} and {b} of the {bf} share the same habit: a whistle at midnight. Both lines at {place} now wait for it before they sleep.
{b} ({bf}) and {a} ({af}) watched each other through the same loophole at {place} for an hour. Neither fired. Neither will explain why.
{b} of the {bf} lost a harmonica in no man's land at {place}. {a} of the {af} found it and has been learning the enemy's songs on it.
A dog crosses no man's land at {place} every night, fed by {a} on one side and {b} on the other. The {af} call it Patrol. The {bf} call it Spy.
{a} ({af}) and {b} ({bf}) were sent out to cut the other side's wire at {place} on the same night. They met in the middle and agreed to go home.
{b} of the {bf} shouted across the wire at {place}, asking for the football scores from home. {a} of the {af} shouted them back. Some of them were even true.
{a} of the {af} lobbed a tin of jam over the wire at {place}. It came back empty, washed, with a flower inside and {b}'s name scratched on the lid.
{a} ({af}) shouted a joke across the wire at {place}. {b} ({bf}) shouted one back. Neither understood the other, and both laughed.
{b} of the {bf} left a loaf of bread on a post at {place}, with a note: 'for whoever is hungry'. {a} took the bread and left a tin of beef.
{a} and {b} spotted each other across a ruined orchard at {place}. Both raised a hand. Both lowered it quickly.
{a} ({af}) heard a mouth organ from the {bf} trench at {place}. {a} knew the tune. {a} sang along under {as} breath.
{b} of the {bf} waved a white rag at {place} to pick up a wounded man. {a} held fire until the man was in.
{a} and {b} sat on opposite sides of a crater at {place} for a long moment. Then {b} nodded and slid out the other way.
A white dog ran between the lines at {place}. {a} ({af}) and {b} ({bf}) both whistled for it. It chose neither.
{b} of the {bf} traded a button for a cigarette with {a} through a hole in the wall at {place}. Both pretended it never happened.
At {place}, {a} ({af}) saw {b} ({bf}) washing a shirt in a puddle. Neither fired, and the shirt was clean by noon.

steps: A rat has started sitting on the ammunition box next to {name}'s bunk. {He} has named it {pet}.
{pet} the rat now waits for {name} at dawn watch every morning. {He} shares crumbs with it. The corporal calls this desertion of rations.
{pet} ran squealing out of the dugout at three in the morning. {name} followed, cursing, seconds before a shell came through the roof. {He} owes {pet} {his} life.
{name} has not seen {pet} for two days. {He} tells everyone rats come and go. {He} still leaves crumbs on the box.
{name} got a letter from {love}. Two pages, one of them only about the weather back home. {He} read that page most.
{name} wrote back to {love} and tore it up three times. The fourth version says almost nothing, which is how {he} knows it is the right one.
No post for {name} this week. {He} checks the sack anyway, every day, and pretends {he} was only looking for tobacco.
A parcel from {love}: socks, a cake gone hard as a brick, and a pressed flower. {name} ate the cake and kept the flower in {item}'s place.
A one-eyed crow landed on the parapet above {name}. The men named it {crow} and said it had chosen {him}.
{crow} the crow follows {name} along the trench now. When {crow} flies off, men duck. They are usually right to.
Somebody in {sector} wanted to shoot {crow} for the pot. {name} stood in front of the rifle. The matter has been dropped.

dog: Biscuit
Shrapnel
Kaiser
Mercy
Lump

steps: A muddy dog crawled into {sector} through the wire. {name} gave it half {his} bread. It has not left {his} side since. The men call it {dog}.
{dog} has learned to carry messages in a tin on its collar. {name} is very proud. {dog} is mainly proud of the biscuits.
{dog} barked at nothing in the dark at four in the morning, and kept barking. A raiding party was twenty yards from the wire. {sector} was ready for them.
{name} hummed an old song from home on sentry. From the other side of the wire, very faintly, someone hummed it back.
{name} sang the first verse tonight, out loud. The other side sang the second. Nobody fired for an hour.
An officer heard about the singing and forbade it. Tonight {name} only whistled the first bar. Across the wire, someone whistled the last.

stranger: a woman in a white dress
two small boys on a bench
an old man with a dog

steps: {name} found a photograph in the mud of no man's land: {stranger}, and a name on the back that is not from {his} side of the wire.
{name} keeps the photograph in {his} pocket next to {item}. {He} says {he} will give it back after the war. Nobody asks to whom.
{name} left the photograph on a stake in the wire at {place}, wrapped in oilcloth. In the morning it was gone. In its place: a single cigarette.

stake: a pocket watch that does not work

steps: {name} won {stake} at cards from a lance corporal in {sector}. The lance corporal wants a rematch.
Rematch. {name} lost everything {he} won, plus {item}. The whole dugout watched.
Third game, by candlelight, with the shelling for a clock. {name} won back {item} and nothing else. {He} says that was all {he} was playing for.
{name} pressed {his} ear to the tunnel wall under {place} and heard it: tapping. Someone is digging toward {him}.
The tapping under {place} is closer. {name} and two others work in silence, in socks, by the light of one candle.
{name} broke through into the enemy gallery at dawn. It was empty. A lamp was still warm. {He} blew it out and placed the charge.
The mine under {place} went up at noon. The whole front felt it. {name} sat at the tunnel mouth afterwards and did not speak until dark.
There is a sniper across the way the men call {foe}. Three helmets went up on sticks today. {foe} hit all three. {name} watched where the shots came from.
{name} lay in the ruins of {place} all day. {foe} did not fire once. Neither did {name}. Both of them know.
At dusk a glint from the ridge. {name} fired once. The front has been quiet ever since, and nobody talks about {foe} any more.
{name} carried in {boy}, who lied about his age to enlist. {boy} kept asking whether his mother would be told.
{boy} has a fever. {name} sits with him after every shift and reads to him from a book with the last pages missing.
