{boy} was put on the hospital train today, alive. He gave {name} a button from his tunic. {name} wears it on {his} own.
{name} learned that {prize} is stored in the cellar at battalion headquarters. {He} has been making careful drawings.
{name} volunteered for a supply run to headquarters. {He} came back with exactly what was ordered and a suspiciously large coat.
The whole of {sector} ate well tonight. {prize} has been reported missing. {name} has been reported as a very good cook.
The line to the battery keeps going dead at the same spot near {place}. {name} suspects it is not the shelling.
{name} crawled out along the wire at night and found the break: neat, cut, recent. Someone is listening in.
{name} laid a second line, deep, by a different route, and left the old one live with false orders on it. Tomorrow the enemy shells an empty farm.
{name} started keeping a diary in the back of a field service book. First entry: "Still here."
{name}'s diary, day nine: "Still here. Soup again. A rat called the Major. Nothing else worth writing, which is the point."
{name} read {his} diary from the start tonight and laughed at how frightened {he} was back then. Then {he} stopped laughing and wrote: "Still here."
{name} borrowed a serial novel from a newspaper bundle. The instalment ends with a locked door and a pistol shot. The next issue is missing.
{name} has asked three carrying parties for the next instalment. So far, the search has produced racing results and an advertisement for boots.
The dugout has begun inventing endings to {name}'s story. The cook's version involves an inheritance; the corporal's involves a disciplinary hearing.
The missing instalment reached {name}. The explanation was so poor that the dugout voted to keep the cook's ending.

record: a waltz with a scratched introduction
a march played slightly too slowly
an operatic duet nobody can translate

steps: A supply man offered {name} a damaged gramophone in exchange for help unloading. {He} accepted before asking whether there were any records.
{name} coaxed the gramophone into turning. It plays {record}, but something knocks once every revolution.
The gramophone stopped knocking after {name} tightened a screw. The dugout applauded the repair halfway through {record}, spoiling the best part.
{name} passed the gramophone to the next section with a note about the screw. By evening, {record} could be heard faintly through the wall.
{name} began a chess game by post with a friend at home. {He} copied the opening move onto the corner of an ordinary letter.
The reply to {name}'s chess move arrived with a long complaint about the weather at home and a note that {his} opponent had taken a pawn.
{name} asked the dugout for advice on the next move. Three men disagreed so fiercely that a second board had to be drawn.
{name} received a letter announcing checkmate. The dugout insists the position was copied incorrectly. {He} has written back asking for another game.
{name} found a blank menu card and wrote the evening ration on it in elaborate handwriting. The bread became 'Bread, in the Army Manner'.
{name}'s menu now circulates before supper. Someone has requested a wine list. The water bucket has been given a vintage.
An officer asked who was writing the menus. {name} admitted it and waited. The officer asked for a copy to send home.
{name} retired the menu after running out of grand names for turnips. The final card reads 'The Usual', underlined twice.
A recruit asked {name} how to write an address. {He} brought paper and began with the largest letters on a ration label.
{name} and the recruit have reached whole words. Lessons take place beside the stove, with spelling corrections from people pretending not to listen.
The recruit wrote a first short letter without {name}'s help. {He} was allowed to check the envelope, but not the contents.
A reply arrived for the recruit. {name} listened while it was read aloud, slowly, without once supplying a word.
A parcel came for {name} that was really meant for another soldier with the same surname. Inside: {gift}. {He} put everything back and kept only the wrapping.
The parcel's address was smudged. {name} took it to the clerk, who found two possible units and no reason to hurry.
{name} caught a supply driver heading for one of the units and handed the parcel over with a note asking for word when it arrived.
A card reached {name}: the parcel had found its owner. The message said thank you, and that {gift} had come just in time.
A new recruit would not eat with the others. {name} left a place at the end of the bench and said nothing about it.
The recruit sat beside {name} at supper but left before the talk began. {name} passed the bread without trying to start a conversation.
The recruit corrected {name}'s account of a football match. It was the longest sentence anyone had heard from that end of the bench.
At supper, the recruit was arguing about football before {name} arrived. {He} had to ask for room on the bench.
{name} found water collecting beneath the gun's cover. {He} sketched a small shelter and took the drawing to the stores.
The stores supplied {name} with shorter boards than requested. The gun shelter has become an exercise in joints and bad language.
{name} finished the shelter. The crew tested every movement of the gun and discovered that the roof needed moving back a hand's width.
The altered shelter passed inspection. {name} found the crew had added a tiny sign: 'No lodgers'. Someone had already left a blanket inside.
{name} was sent to examine a pump that worked only when struck. {He} asked the men to stop striking it long enough to listen.
The pump's fault proved to be a worn fitting. {name} made a replacement from scrap while the men returned to bailing by hand.
{name}'s replacement fitting held, but the intake kept clogging. {He} fitted a rough screen and stayed through a full shift to watch it.
The pump ran without help. {name} left a short maintenance note and took away the hammer everyone had been using on it.
A patient at the aid post asked {name} for a pencil. By evening, the wall beside the stretcher bore a drawing of a kitchen.
The patient has added a stove and three chairs to the kitchen drawing. {name} asks about each detail while changing the dressing.
Before evacuation, the patient asked {name} to tear the drawing from the paper lining the wall. {He} managed it without losing the stove.
A note arrived from the hospital: the kitchen drawing survived the journey. The patient intends to show the builder exactly where the extra chair should go.
{name} took a wrong turn at two identical trench junctions. {He} decided the route needed names that could be remembered under pressure.
{name} marked the first junction with a spoon and the second with a boot sole. Other runners have begun using the names in their directions.
Someone removed the spoon from {name}'s junction to eat supper. {He} retrieved it and nailed it above comfortable reaching height.
A new runner delivered a message using Spoon Corner and Boot Turn without hesitation. {name} drew both markers on the official route sketch.

mark: a gap beneath a roof beam
a crack in an old stone wall

steps: {name} noticed regular flashes from {mark}. The position looks obvious enough to make {him} suspicious.
{name} watched {mark} through another shift. The flash returns at the same angle, even when nothing else moves.
A second observer helped {name} confirm the trick: a piece of glass, placed to draw fire. The real watching point must be elsewhere.
{name} marked {mark} as a decoy on the observation sketch. {He} passed the warning on and began examining the less obvious gaps.
{name} heard a faint second conversation on the telephone line. Headquarters said only one line was connected.
The extra voice came back during {name}'s test. It was talking about potatoes, which made enemy spies an unlikely explanation.
{name} traced the fault to two badly insulated wires touching near a junction. One of them belonged to the supply office.
With the wires separated, {name}'s telephone carried only orders again. The section misses hearing what was for supper before it was served.
{name} obtained a recipe for {dish}. The instructions assume a kitchen, a steady fire and ingredients that do not arrive in sacks.
{name} tried a small batch of {dish}. The bottom burned before the middle cooked. The tasting committee ate the edges and requested patience.
For the second attempt, {name} raised the pot above the hottest part of the fire. The smell brought volunteers before help was requested.
{name} served {dish} to the whole section. Someone asked whether it would appear again. {He} told them to speak to the people delivering the flour.
{name} was asked to arrange a gathering for men who did not want a sermon. {He} asked what they did want and wrote down the answers.
The list for {name}'s gathering contains a poem, a song and a request for five minutes without orders. All three seem possible.
{name} held the gathering in a shelter after supper. The poem was read badly, the song went better, and nobody interrupted the silence.
A man asked {name} to hold another gathering. This time, the request came with a folded poem and an offer to read it.
{name} discovered three men claiming the next place on the leave roster. Each had a different copy of the list.
{name} checked the leave claims against old orders. Two changes had never been copied across; one name had disappeared at a fold in the paper.
The corrected leave list went up under {name}'s signature. Nobody liked every decision, but everyone could see how it had been reached.
The first man left under the corrected roster. {name} watched the departure, then made a second copy of the list before anything else could happen to it.
{name} bought a small phrasebook from a passing soldier. The first useful sentence appears after six pages about hiring a carriage.
{name} practised asking for bread in the local language. The dugout supplied an audience and several confidently incorrect pronunciations.
A local carter understood {name}'s request for bread, then explained that the same sentence sounded very much like a request for a beard.
{name} corrected the phrasebook in pencil. The carter added three useful expressions and refused to translate a fourth suggested by the corporal.
{name} began repairing a blanket with scraps from ruined clothing. The first patch is a different colour from everything else.
Word of {name}'s blanket spread. A strip of lining and a square from an old scarf arrived without explanation.
{name} finished the blanket using six kinds of cloth. The men can identify most of the donors by the patches alone.
The patched blanket kept {name} warm through the night. In the morning, a neighbour arrived with another torn blanket and an optimistic expression.
{name}'s spoon vanished during supper. {He} scratched a mark into a replacement and began keeping a closer eye on the washing bucket.
A second spoon disappeared. {name} searched the washing area and found a gap behind the board where everyone left cutlery to dry.
{name} lifted the board. The gap contained seven spoons, a button and a pencil people had blamed the quartermaster for losing.
The recovered spoons were laid out for collection. {name} took the original and repaired the gap before the next meal.
{name} agreed to sit for a portrait drawn by a man with a piece of charcoal. The first result made {him} look twice {his} age.
The artist tried again while {name} read a letter. The new portrait was better, though the ears became the subject of discussion.
{name} sent the portrait home after asking the artist to leave the ears alone. A photograph would have cost more than {he} could spare.
A reply from home thanked {name} for the portrait. It is already on the mantelpiece, where the family apparently recognises the ears.
{name}'s left boot has opened at the toe. {He} tied it with string and walked as if nothing had happened.
{name} asked every man in the squad if anyone had a spare pair of boots. Nobody had. One man offered {swap} as a sign of sympathy.
A supply truck stopped at the dump. {name} got in the line early and got to the front. The boots were two sizes too big, and {he} wore them with three pairs of socks.
{name}'s new boots have a way of squeaking on the duckboards. The sergeant says it is better than not hearing {him} at all.
A thin gray kitten wandered into {sector} and hid in {name}'s helmet. {He} gave it a spoon of condensed milk.
The kitten now follows {name} everywhere. The squad calls it {cat}, and {name} pretends not to care.
{cat} caught its first rat today and laid it at {name}'s feet. {name} said thank you and buried it quietly.
{cat} has moved into the dugout for good. It sleeps on {name}'s chest and is not asked to leave.
{name} started drawing a map of {his} village on the dugout wall with a piece of charcoal. {He} started with the church.
Every evening {name} adds a street or a house to the wall map. The squad has begun to point out what is missing.
A man from the next trench came by to look at {name}'s map. He turned out to be from the next village. They talked for hours.
The wall map is almost finished. {name} added the last thing today: a tiny dot, with a name next to it, for the house {he} will return to.
{name} has been given a small jar of sourdough starter by the cook, with strict instructions to keep it alive. It lives in {his} coat.
The starter bubbled all night in {name}'s coat. {He} slept badly, but the jar is doing well.
{name} baked the first loaf over the stove today. It was flat, dense, and slightly sour. The squad ate every crumb.
{name} gave a piece of the starter to a man in the next dugout. 'Keep it warm,' {he} said. 'It likes company.'
{name} found a packet of seeds in a ruined house and put them in a tin of soil on the parapet at {sector}.
Two green shoots have come up in {name}'s tin. The squad has agreed not to step near it.
The shoots in {name}'s tin have grown a hand tall. A passing officer stopped, looked, and said nothing.
A small yellow flower opened in {name}'s tin at {sector} this morning. Half the squad came to see it.
{name}'s watch stopped at ten past four. {He} has carried it ever since, as if it were still running.
{name} asked the sapper to look at the watch. The sapper opened it with a pin and said: it is not broken, it is tired.
The sapper cleaned the watch with a feather and a drop of oil. After an hour, it started to tick.
{name} wore the watch on the fire step today. It is four minutes slow, and {he} would not change it for a gold one.
{name} found a torn book about the night sky in a ruined library. It has no cover, but it has pictures of stars.
On night watch {name} found the bright star in the book and told the sentry beside {him} its name.
Now half the squad can name three stars. {name} insists on testing them before dawn watch, in a whisper.
A cloudy night. {name} could not see a single star, and recited them all from memory instead.
The squad has started a game: guess how many letters will come in the next mail. {name} guessed seven. It was twelve.
{name} bet {prize} that the mail would be late. The mail was on time. {He} paid with grace and a sigh.
{name} guessed the exact number of letters this time. The squad accused {him} of reading the bag.
The mail game has become a tradition. {name} keeps the score on a board by the stove, and nobody trusts the score.

weather.label: Rain
diary: It rained from dusk to dawn. The communication trenches are knee-deep again and the duckboards float.
Rain all day, steady and patient. The mud has swallowed two more boots and a mule.
Rain found the seams in every roof. Men moved their bedding in small circles, following the last dry patches.
The rain filled yesterday's footprints before the morning carrying parties arrived. Every path had to be learnt again.
The rain came sideways at dawn and straight down by noon. The sandbags along the top of the trench have turned to soup.
Rain all night. The sentries stood in water up to their shins and swapped every hour to save their feet.
Rain drummed on the tin roofs of the dugouts until nobody could hear the guns. Some men called it the best sleep in weeks.
The rain washed the chalk off the trench signs. Three runners got lost before noon.
Rain, then more rain. The latrines overflowed into the support trench, and nobody wants to talk about it.
The rain softened the trench walls until they began to slump. Every spare hand was out with a shovel, digging them back into shape.

weather.label: Fog
titles: A day off for the snipers
diary: Fog sat in the valley until noon. Sentries on both sides fired at shapes that were not there.
A grey wall of fog from dawn to dusk. Patrols went out blind and came back counting each other twice.
Fog erased the landmarks along the front. Orders at trench junctions were repeated at arm's length.
The fog thinned in strips and closed again. Sentries caught brief views of ground they could not keep in sight.
Fog so thick the sentries could not see their own wire. Both sides fired at sounds all night.
The fog lifted for ten minutes at noon and showed a whole new trench the enemy had dug. Then it came down again.
Runners walked into the wrong trenches all day in the fog. One came back with a cup of the enemy's coffee and a story.
Fog lay in no man's land like milk in a bowl. Patrols went out and came back with nothing to report.
In the fog every voice sounded close. The men whispered all day, even back in the reserve line.
The fog stayed past noon. Snipers on both sides had a day off and did not know what to do with it.

weather.label: Frost
diary: A hard frost. The mud froze into ridges sharp enough to cut boots, and the wire sang in the wind.
Ice on the water in the shell holes. The men stamped their feet all night to keep the blood moving.
Frost stiffened canvas and clothing overnight. Every buckle and knot took longer to work with numb fingers.
Water froze in shallow containers. The first task of the morning was making enough heat to begin the ordinary tasks.
Frost on the wire this morning, white and sharp. For an hour no man's land looked almost beautiful.
The mud froze hard in the night. For once the men could walk without sinking, and the carrying parties made record time.
Frost cracked the water in the buckets. The tea came up from the kitchens with ice floating in it.
The frost made every footstep crunch. Patrols stayed in; the enemy would have heard them coming a mile off.
Men woke with frost in their hair and their boots frozen to the floor. Nobody complained about the stove smoke today.
The frost held all day. Rifles had to be warmed under coats before the dawn watch.

weather.label: Clear
titles: A long view across the wire
diary: A clear, cold day. Good for snipers and observers, bad for everyone else.
Blue sky over the front for the first time in a week. Both sides used it to shell each other with great accuracy.
Clear weather exposed paths usually hidden by haze. Carrying parties waited for darkness rather than risk the open stretches.
The sky stayed clear through the evening. Laundry dried behind the lines while observers watched the roads ahead.
A clear day, and every periscope on both sides was up. Nobody raised a head above the parapet.
The sky was so clear that the men could see a church spire far behind the enemy lines. Some of them stared at it for a long time.
Clear weather baked the top of the mud into a crust. Under it, the mud waited.
The sun came out and half the trench hung their socks on the wire behind the line. It looked like a country fair.
Clear skies brought out the airplanes. The men watched them circle like crows over the ridge.
A blue sky all day. It was so quiet that a lark sang over no man's land, and both sides stopped to listen.

weather.label: Storm
diary: Thunder all night, and nobody could tell which of it was the sky.
A storm broke over the ridge at midnight. Lightning showed the whole front for a heartbeat at a time: wire, craters, men.
The storm drove water sideways beneath the shelters. Loose boards became urgent work, whatever the duty roster said.
Lightning revealed the ground in sudden fragments. Between flashes, the dark seemed thicker than before.
Thunder and gunfire mixed all night until nobody could tell which was which.
Lightning lit up no man's land like a flare. Both sides ducked every time.
The storm blew the roof off the cookhouse dugout. Lunch was late, wet, and served with an apology.
The storm flooded the lower trenches by midnight. Men slept sitting up on the fire step.
A storm in the night tore the canvas off the aid post. The orderlies held it down with their own bodies until dawn.
The storm passed by noon and left the trenches smelling of wet earth and smoke. Every dugout was opened to air out.

weather.label: Wind
diary: A cold wind from the east carried the smell of the other trenches: smoke, lime and cooking.
Gale all day. Sandbags slid, roofs lifted, and the gas sentries watched the wind direction like hawks.
Wind pulled smoke flat above the trenches. Men checked shelter ropes and kept a close watch on changes in direction.
A hard wind made every loose sheet of metal audible. Conversation moved into doorways and around the sheltered sides of walls.
The wind blew the smell of the enemy's breakfast across the wire. Everyone was hungry by eight.
The wind carried voices across no man's land all day. The men heard the enemy laughing at a joke nobody here understood.
A hard wind blew grit into every rifle. Each one was cleaned twice before dark.
The wind tore a letter out of a soldier's hand and carried it over the wire. Somebody over there is reading it now.
The wind rattled the empty cans hung on the wire all night. Sentries fired at nothing three times before dawn.
The wind turned in the night and blew each side's smoke back into its own trenches. Both lines coughed until morning.

firstWave: {name} is one of the first hundred to answer the call. {He} wears the ribbon of the First Wave.
Volunteer number {n}. The quartermaster pinned the First Wave ribbon on {name}'s tunic and said: 'Don't let the mud have it.'
{name} was among the first hundred through the depot gates. The First Wave ribbon is the only clean thing {he} owns.
The colonel shook hands with the first hundred, one by one. {name} was number {n}. {He} still remembers how stiff the colonel's glove felt.
First Wave. {name} signed when the ink on the posters was still fresh. {He} keeps the ribbon wrapped in oilcloth with {item}.
{name} answered the first call, number {n} on the rolls. Somebody chalked the number on {his} helmet. It has not washed off yet.
{name} was in the first hundred. The old hands in {sector} call them 'the early birds', and not always kindly.
Number {n} on the early rolls: {name}. The First Wave ribbon arrived with instructions about where to sew it and no needle.
{name} received the First Wave ribbon. {He} checked the stitching twice before putting the tunic back on.
One of the first hundred, {name} was given the First Wave ribbon. {He} wrapped the paper that came with it in oilcloth to keep it safe.
The First Wave ribbon marked {name} as an early volunteer. At {sector}, a newcomer asked what those first days had been like.
{name}, volunteer number {n}, received the First Wave ribbon. The quartermaster pronounced the name wrong; {he} corrected it for the record.
The first hundred were recognised, and {name} was among them. {He} wrote the news on the back of an unfinished letter.
{name}'s First Wave ribbon drew a question at supper. {He} remembered the queue at the depot more clearly than the speech.
As one of the first hundred volunteers, {name} received the First Wave ribbon. A neighbour lent the needle and supervised every stitch.

quirks: never sits with {his} back to the parapet
writes everything down in a tiny notebook
whistles the same four notes over and over
laughs at exactly the wrong moments
is superstitious about the number three
draws portraits of the men in the margins of letters
will not eat before a raid
is always the first one awake
reads the same book over and over
waiting: a younger sister who sends drawings
a sweetheart who has stopped writing
a mother who sets a place for {him} at every meal
a wife and a daughter {he} has never met
an old father who runs the family shop alone
an old neighbor who promised to keep {his} garden alive
a girl from the dance hall, maybe
five brothers, all on other fronts
a grandmother who prays for both armies
a fiancée who wears {his} ring on a chain
a teacher who said {he} would amount to nothing
twin brothers too young to enlist
a landlady who kept {his} room exactly as it was

enlistLate: {name} arrived on Day {day} as a replacement. The men in {sector} had been fighting for {daysIn} days already and looked at {his} clean boots like a rumour from another world.
By the time {name} reached {sector}, the war was {daysIn} days old and had its own habits. {He} learned the first one within the hour: keep your head down.
{name} came up with a draft of replacements on Day {day}. Nobody asked {his} name until the third night. After that, everyone knew it.
The sergeant gave {name} a dead man's blanket and a living man's job. That is how replacements start, on Day {day} or any other.
{name}, a {trade} from {home}, was sent forward on Day {day} to fill a gap in {sector}. The gap had a name once. Nobody says it.
"You're late," said the corporal when {name} arrived on Day {day}. "Everyone's late. Get a spade."
{name} arrived with the Day {day} draft, carrying {item} and the news from home, which was old by the time {he} told it.
The old hands of {sector} have been here since Day 1. {name} has been here since Day {day}. In a trench, that difference already feels like years.
{name} walked into {sector} on Day {day} and asked where the war was. A shell answered before anyone else could.
On Day {day} {name} took a post at {sector} that had been empty for two nights. {He} did not ask why. {He} {quirk}, and the men liked {him} for it.
On Day {day}, {name} arrived during an argument about a missing spoon. The war already had matters more urgent than introductions.
{name} joined the replacements on Day {day}. An old hand checked {his} pack straps before asking {his} name.
Day {day}: {name} reached {sector} with a full packet of cigarettes. Learning everyone's name proved remarkably easy.
The draft reached {sector} on Day {day}. {name} was shown which board tipped, which roof leaked and which promises to ignore.
{name} came up on Day {day} carrying news from {home}. A man interrupted to ask whether the railway clock had been repaired.
Day {day}. The corporal put {name} beside a veteran and said to copy everything except the language.
{name} arrived on Day {day} and found the section asleep. The welcome had to wait until somebody needed the kettle.
After {daysIn} days of war, {sector} had a place for everything. On Day {day}, the men rearranged a shelf to make a place for {name}.
raceWin: Day {day}. The {us} took {objective}. From the heights {name} could see the whole {them} line, and for the first time the war looked winnable.
{objective} fell to the {us} at dusk. {name} helped drag the guns up the slope and slept that night on ground nobody else had held for years.
The {us} flag went up over {objective}. {name} did not cheer. {He} sat down on a sandbag and ate {his} ration slowly, like a man with time again.
Word came down the line: {objective} is ours. {name} shook hands with a corporal {he} had never spoken to. Today, everyone was a friend.
{name} walked the captured trenches of {objective} and found the enemy's cooking pots still warm. {He} took a spoon as a souvenir.
{objective} is in {us} hands. {name} watched the map being corrected and wondered how such a small pencil mark could take so much work.
News that the {us} had taken {objective} reached {name} during supper. The same stew suddenly tasted better.
The {us} secured {objective}. {name} helped pass the news along the line, checking each time that {he} had heard correctly.
Victory at {objective}. {name} let {him}self talk about leave for the first time in days.
The {us} took {objective}, and the orders at {sector} changed before the cheering ended. {name} shouldered another load.
On Day {day}, {objective} passed to the {us}. {name} wrote the name in {his} diary with unusual care.
{objective} has been won. {name} listened as the corporal read the news twice, once for the men just off watch.
The report confirmed the {us} victory at {objective}. {name} folded the paper so the headline stayed on the outside.
raceLose: Day {day}. {objective} fell to the {them}. {name} watched their flag go up on the heights and dug {his} trench a little deeper.
The {them} hold {objective} now, and they can see straight into {sector}. {name} has learned to walk bent double.
{objective} is lost. {name} heard the news from a runner, said nothing, and checked {his} rifle twice. There will be another race.
From {objective} the {them} guns have a clear view. {name} wrote to {waiting} that night and said only: 'We will take it back.'
The sergeant read out the order: {objective} has fallen, hold the line. {name} looked at the new recruits coming up the road and counted them.
The {them} took {objective}. {name} watched the officer move a pin on the map and ask for more digging tools.
News of the loss of {objective} reached {sector} with the rations. {name} ate while listening to the revised orders.
{objective} is in {them} hands. {name} stopped arguing about the next watch and went to check the stores.
Day {day}: {objective} was lost. {name} wrote down the news without trying to explain it.
The report confirmed that the {them} held {objective}. {name} read the last line twice, looking for something the first reading had missed.
After the loss of {objective}, {name} helped stack spare sandbags at {sector}. Nobody asked when they would be needed.
The {them} won {objective}. In {sector}, {name} listened to three explanations and trusted none of them.
{objective} fell to the {them}. {name} kept the newspaper; {he} wanted to remember exactly what had been promised beforehand.
raceHero: The {us} needed one more rifle to take {objective}. {name} was that rifle. From today, they call {him} the Hero of {objective}.
{name} arrived on the very day the {us} reached the heights of {objective}. The men swear {he} tipped the balance. The colonel agreed and wrote it down.
The {us} victory at {objective} made {name} a hero. The men still made {him} wait in the ration queue, which came as a relief.
{name} was named Hero of {objective}. Asked for a few words, {he} gave the names of the people who had helped.
The citation credited {name} with tipping the struggle for {objective}. {He} asked for a copy to send to {home}.
Word spread that {name} had made the difference at {objective}. By evening, the story had grown larger than anything {he} remembered.
{name} became the Hero of {objective}. A recruit asked to shake {his} hand, and neither knew what to say afterwards.
The {us} celebrated {name}'s part in winning {objective}. {He} sat through the praise with a piece of ration bread still in {his} pocket.
The honour for {objective} was read aloud beside {name}. When it was over, someone quietly handed {him} the tea that had been kept warm.
{name} received the title Hero of {objective}. {He} wrote home about it, then added that {he} still needed socks.
transfer: {name} asked to leave the {oldRole}s and serve as a {role}. The sergeant looked at {him} for a long time, then signed the paper without a word.
Orders came through: {name} is a {role} now. {He} handed in {his} old kit and kept only {item}.
{name} transferred to the {role}s. The men in {sector} said they would miss {him}. {He} is only three dugouts away.
After what happened at {place}, {name} asked to serve as a {role}. Nobody argued.
The {role}s took {name} in on a busy morning in {sector}. By noon {he} had learned the first rule of the job, and by evening the second.
{name} reported for duty as a {role}. The new kit was heavier than the explanation of how to use it.
The transfer made {name} a {role}. {He} spent the first hour learning where everything belonged, including {him}self.
{name} left the work of a {oldRole} to become a {role}. Someone from the old section came over to see how it was going.
Now serving as a {role}, {name} discovered that being experienced at the front did not prevent being new at the job.
{name}'s transfer to the role of {role} was approved. The quartermaster wanted every borrowed item back before issuing anything else.
{name} became a {role} today. {He} wrote the change in a letter home, then crossed out the explanation and tried again.
Orders assigned {name} to work as a {role}. The first lesson began with what not to touch.
The new duty roster listed {name} as a {role}. {He} kept checking the old roster until someone took it down.
exchanged: {name} came back in a prisoner exchange at dawn, thinner, with a borrowed coat and {item}. {He} will not talk about the cage.
A white flag, a handshake in the mud, and {name} walked back across no man's land in an exchange of prisoners. The whole squad cheered {him} in.
{name} was traded back for an enemy officer. {He} says the other side's coffee is worse than ours, and that is the only thing {he} says.
{name} returned in a prisoner exchange. At the first meal, {he} pocketed half the bread before remembering where {he} was.
The exchange brought {name} back to {sector}. Everyone had questions. The corporal sent them away and fetched a chair.
{name} crossed back during the prisoner exchange with a list of names to pass on. {He} would not rest until someone had copied it.
Returned from captivity, {name} asked for paper before tobacco. There was news that needed to reach {home}.
{name} came back through the exchange with boots that did not match. The quartermaster found a pair without asking for a form.
At the prisoner exchange, {name} recognised a voice before recognising the uniform. {He} finally let go of the bundle under {his} arm.
{name} returned from captivity carrying a spoon worn almost flat. {He} declined a replacement.
The prisoner exchange restored {name} to the rolls. At {sector}, someone had to explain where the dugout had moved.

{nA} {A} and {nB} {B} went over the parapet under {weather}. All of them were heading for {loc}.
Under {weather}, {loc} drew them in from both sides: {nA} {A}, {nB} {B}, faces blackened with burnt cork.
openSolo: Under {weather}, the {S} sent a raiding party to {loc}. The other side sent nobody.
The {S} went out to {loc} under {weather} and found no enemy waiting. Only the place itself.
Under {weather}, the {S} slipped through the wire toward {loc}. On the other side, nobody had volunteered.
The {S} went out to {loc} under {weather} and found the enemy had stayed in bed.
snipe: The first shot came from {a} before anyone saw a thing; {t} was hit.
{a} fired first, from somewhere nobody could see. {t} was the target.
{a} fired once from the dark before anyone knew where the dark was. {t} went down.
One shot, from a spot {a} had picked hours earlier. {t} was out of it before the fight began.
shell: {a} cranked the field telephone and a shell landed square on {t}.
The first blow came from the sky: {a} called the guns, and {t} was right under them.
{a} whispered map numbers into the field telephone. A minute later the ground under {t} stood up.
{a} called down the guns, and for once they listened. {t} was in the wrong crater.
jam: In the wet, the gun of {a} jammed at the worst moment.
{a} swore at a jammed gun while the rain hissed on the barrel.
The gun of {a} coughed once and stopped. Mud in the breech, at the worst possible moment.
{a} hammered at a jammed bolt with the heel of a hand while the fight went on without it.
mvp: {a} fought like three men and put {n} of the enemy out of the fight.
The name on every lip afterwards: {a}, with {n} enemies down.
{a} was everywhere at once and put {n} of the enemy out of the fight.
When it was counted afterwards, {a} alone had stopped {n} of them.
heal: {a} kept crawling between the craters and dragged {t} back into cover.
Through all of it, {a} worked on the wounded, {t} first.
{a} crawled out under fire, found {t} by the groaning and dragged {t} into the nearest hole.
{a} dressed the wounds of {t} in a shell hole by touch alone. A light would have killed them both.
rout: In exchange {round} the {X} broke and fell back.
The {X} could take no more and ran for their own wire.
In exchange {round} the {X} ran out of nerve before they ran out of ammunition, and fell back.
Exchange {round} broke the {X}. They went back the way they had come, only faster.
hazard: The ground fought back: mines, gas pockets and falling walls. {t} paid for it.
Old mines and a collapsing wall caught {t}.
The ground had its own traps, older than the raid: a buried mine, a pocket of gas, a wall that chose that moment. {t} found them.
Not every wound came from the enemy. The place itself bit {t}.
noLoss: Everyone came back on their own feet.
Roll call afterwards was short and complete.
For once, everyone who went out came back on their own legs.

By first light the {W} were digging in at {loc}. {perk}
The {W} took {loc} wall by wall and held the last one at dawn. {perk}

The raiders broke against {loc} and the {W} stayed put. {perk}
stalemate: Neither side could hold the ground. {loc} is contested.
By morning both parties had pulled back. {loc} belongs to nobody.
Both sides left {loc} before dawn, and both claimed it in their reports.
At sunrise {loc} belonged to the crows.
solo: Nobody came to stop them. The {W} walked into {loc} and stayed. {perk}
The {W} took {loc} without firing a shot and still cannot quite believe it. {perk}

Nobody fought the {S} at {loc}. The place did it for them, and they came home empty-handed.
The {S} reached {loc} and found it did not want them. They were back before dawn.
empty: Field HQ asked for volunteers for {loc}. Nobody stepped forward. The rats keep it for now.
Field HQ waited all day for names for {loc}. None came. The crows have it for now.
Nobody went to {loc}. The mud there stays undisturbed a while longer.

{a} was in the thick of it and dropped one of them.
{a} got close enough to put one of them out of the fight with a rifle butt.
{a} stopped one of the enemy cold and kept the rest of the party alive doing it.

Nobody fired more, or better, than {a}.
{a} gave them more trouble than anyone, even if nobody stayed down for it.
{a} fired, crawled and fired again. Nobody fought harder that night.

{name} went out to {loc} {withMates}. The {them} broke first.
{name} crawled out to {loc} {withMates} with a blackened face and a sharpened spade. The {us} came back winners.
Night raid on {loc} {withMates}. {name} remembers the noise, the dark, and the moment the {them} gave way.
{name} went through the wire toward {loc} {withMates}. By dawn the {us} had it.

At {sector} a round caught {name} below the ribs. {He} sat down slowly against the trench wall and said, quite calmly, that it hurt.

{name} took a bullet in the side at {sector}. {His} friends laid {him} on a door and walked very carefully.
bulletCrit: A sniper's bullet hit {name} at {sector}. The medics worked on {him} in the bottom of the trench and shouted for a stretcher.

A bullet hit {name} in the neck at {sector}. The medic kept two fingers pressed on the wound all the way down the trench.
{name} was hit through the stomach at {sector}. The bearers ran with the stretcher and did not stop to rest.

A bullet went into {name}'s chest just under the heart at {sector}. The medic said not to give {him} water, and then said nothing more.
{name} was hit twice at {sector}, once in the leg and once in the side. The second wound is the bad one.

At {sector} a round went through {name}'s lung. Every breath had a sound in it that the men will not forget.

wardBed: {name} spent the day in bed with {his} leg propped up. The orderly changed the dressing and said it was healing the way it should.
Another quiet day in the ward for {name}. {He} counted the cracks in the ceiling and got to forty-one.
{name} slept most of the day. When {he} woke, someone had left a cup of tea on the crate beside the bed.

{name} spent the day writing a letter home and tearing it up. By evening there were five pieces of paper on the blanket.

{name} lay on a stretcher under a canvas sheet and watched the orderlies carry men in and out. Nobody had time to talk.

{name} drifted in and out on the stretcher. Every time {he} woke, the line for the beds seemed longer.

{name} spent the day on a stretcher counting the bearers who went past. Forty-three. None of them stopped.
A medic brought {name} half a cup of soup and a promise. The soup was real.
{name} lay on the stretcher and listened to the surgeon working inside. {He} tried not to guess what each sound meant.
Someone moved {name}'s stretcher out of the doorway. It was the most anyone did for {him} all day, and {he} was grateful.
{name} lay on a stretcher and watched the sky turn from grey to pink. A medic brought a cup of tea and said nothing.
A medic checked on {name} at noon. The wound looked better, but there was still no bed.
{name} spent the day on a stretcher at the aid post, reading the same page of a torn book six times.
{name} gave {his} biscuit to the boy on the next stretcher. The boy ate it and cried a little.
{name} waited on a stretcher for a bed that did not come. The medics changed {his} bandage and promised again.
The bearers stepped over {name}'s stretcher all day. Each one said sorry. {name} said it was fine.
{name} was moved on the stretcher into the shade. It was the best thing that happened all day.
{name} lay on a stretcher beside the aid post and counted the men carried past. {He} stopped at fifty.
wardTrench: {name} lay in a dugout at {sector} with a rolled coat under {his} head. There was no stretcher and no bed. A medic looked in when {he} could.

{name} was propped against the trench wall at {sector}. {He} drank what water the others could spare and stared at the sandbags overhead.
{name} spent the day lying on the trench floor at {sector}, wrapped in two coats. The squad stepped over {him} carefully, every time.
{name} is still waiting at {sector} for a stretcher. The men brought {him} the best of the rations and pretended it was an accident.
No medic came to {sector} today. {name} changed {his} own bandage with a strip of shirt and a lot of swearing.
{name} lay in a corner of the trench at {sector} and counted the bearers who passed by. None of them had room.
The squad at {sector} made {name} a bed out of empty sandbags and a ration box. It is not much. It is better than the floor.
{name} stayed in the trench at {sector} with a dressing on {his} wound. A medic passed by twice and promised to come back.
No stretcher came for {name}. {He} sat against the trench wall at {sector} with a canteen and a cough.
{name} was left to rest at {sector}, propped on a pile of sandbags. The squad brought {him} hot water.
{name} had a bandage and nothing else. {He} spent the day at {sector} watching the sky and waiting for the medic.
A medic cleaned {name}'s wound at {sector} and moved on to the next man. {name} understood. There were so many.
{name} slept at {sector} on a groundsheet with {his} coat as a pillow. The squad kept their voices down.
Nobody had time for {name} today. {He} pulled a blanket tight at {sector} and waited for it to pass.
{name} lay in the trench at {sector} until dark. A medic came at last, changed the dressing, and asked if {he} had eaten.
wardLight: {name} wore a fresh bandage at {sector} and was told to rest. {He} rested for about an hour.
{name} sat out the day with a bandaged arm, cleaning every rifle within reach. It was the only job the medic would allow.
A medic checked {name}'s dressing at {sector} and said {he} would be back on {his} feet soon. {He} was already trying to stand.
{name} was on light duty: bandaged, bored and in charge of the kettle.
{name} spent the day with {his} arm in a sling, writing letters for men who cannot write.
The medic told {name} to keep the bandage clean. {name} has been guarding it like a medal.
{name} was put on light duty at {sector}: peeling potatoes, sorting mail, and complaining.
{name} sat on an ammunition box at {sector} with a bandaged leg and gave advice to everyone who passed. Nobody asked for it.
{name} was told to rest at {sector}. {He} cleaned {his} rifle three times and then started on someone else's.
With a bandaged hand, {name} could not hold a rifle, so {he} peeled potatoes at {sector} instead. The squad thanked {him} loudly.
{name} sat in the sun at {sector} with a fresh bandage, pretending to be unwell. The sergeant pretended to believe {him}.
The medic told {name} to stay out of the line for a day. {He} spent it sorting buttons into piles.
{name} was kept out of the trench with a sore arm. {He} spent the day rereading old letters and drinking tea.
A bandage on {his} leg kept {name} from walking far. {He} sat on an ammunition box and told the same story to everyone who passed.
{name} was ordered to rest. {He} fell asleep on the fire step with {his} boots on and was not woken.

wardMissing: Nobody at {sector} has seen {name} since the last patrol. {His} bunk is still made.

No word on {name}. A runner went to ask in the next sector and came back with nothing.

{name} is missing. A man in the next trench says {he} heard someone singing out in no man's land after dark.

A flare, boots, a short fight in the dark at {sector}. {name} was killed before the rest of the squad was even awake.
The {side} raiders were in and out in two minutes. At {sector} they left {name} behind, dead on the duckboards.
nightRaidHurt: On the way back from the night raid a flare went up. {name} was caught in the open and hit before reaching the wire.
{name} made it into the enemy trench and out again, but a machine gun swept no man's land on the way home. {name} crawled the last yards.
The raid was quick, the way back was not. {name} snagged on the wire and took a bullet before the others pulled {name} free.
{name} came back from the night raid on two stretcher poles. Nobody is sure which side fired the shot.
nightRaidBack: {name} went over with the night raiders, found the enemy trench empty at that spot, and came back with a bag of their biscuits.
Night raid. {name} crossed no man's land, saw the enemy sentry too late to reach, and came back without a scratch. Next time, says {name}.
{name} joined the raid, lay in a shell hole for an hour while the flares burned, and made it home. That counts as a good night out here.
{name} came back from the raid with mud to the eyebrows and an enemy helmet as a souvenir.
nightRaidFell: {name} went over with the night raiders and never came back. The flare caught {name} on the wire, halfway home.
The raid was over in minutes. On the way back a machine gun swept no man's land, and {name} did not reach the parapet.
{name} made it into the enemy trench and out again. Twenty yards from home, a single shot ended it.
The squad counted heads when the raiders came back. {name} was missing. At dawn they saw {name} lying by the wire.
{name} was the last raider out of the enemy trench, covering the others. The others made it home. {name} did not.
firstThousand: The clerk counted the names twice. {name} is number {n} of the first thousand to answer the call, and wears the ribbon of the First Thousand.
A thousand names now stand in the regimental book. {name} is number {n}. The sergeant pinned the ribbon of the First Thousand on without a speech.
{name} got a narrow grey ribbon today, the ribbon of the First Thousand. Number {n}. The men who came later will ask about it.
The company read out the roll of the First Thousand at the dawn watch. {name} answered to number {n}.
dogArrive: {aBreedC} came up the line with the ration party and would not leave {name}'s side. {name} named the dog {dog}. The sergeant pretended not to see.
{name} found a muddy {breed} shivering under a duckboard and shared {his} bread. Now the dog follows {him} everywhere. {name} calls it {dog}.
{aBreedC} wandered in from no man's land at dawn, wet and hungry. It chose {name}. {name} gave it a name: {dog}.
The quartermaster had {aBreed} pup nobody wanted. {name} took it and called it {dog}. The whole squad already spoils it.
dog: {dog} caught a rat as big as itself and laid it at {name}'s boots. The squad cheered.
{dog} slept curled against {name}'s legs all night. It was the warmest {name} has been in weeks.
{dog} growled at the dark long before anyone heard a sound. {name} woke the post. The dog was right.
{name} shared {his} tin of beef with {dog}. Half for {him}, half for the dog. The dog finished first.
{dog} carried a message tube in its collar from {sector} to the next trench and back. Nobody taught it that.
{dog} stole a sausage from the cook. The cook chased it down the trench. {name} paid for the sausage.
When the shelling started, {dog} pressed itself flat against {name}'s side and did not move until it stopped.
{name} taught {dog} to sit and to stay. {dog} learned to stay. Sitting is still up for debate.
{dog} barked at a flare and then looked very proud of itself. {name} had to hold its mouth shut.
The new men are scared of the dark. {dog} walks along the fire step and lets each of them pat its head.
{dog} found {name}'s lost glove buried in the mud and brought it back, chewed but warm.
{name} wrote home about {dog}. Half the letter was about the dog. The other half was about the dog too.
{dog} chased a rat into a dugout and came out with an officer's cap. {name} returned the cap. Quietly.
{dog} sat on the parapet step and watched no man's land like a sentry. {name} pulled it down. Twice.
The medic checked {dog}'s paws for cuts and wrapped one in a bandage. {dog} now limps only when someone is looking.
{dog} dug a hole in the trench wall. {name} filled it in. {dog} dug it again. The war goes on.
{name} could not sleep. {dog} put its head on {his} chest and stayed there until dawn.
{dog} ran to the ration party and came back with a whole loaf. Nobody asked where it came from.
A soldier from another squad offered three cigarettes for {dog}. {name} said no. The dog is not for sale.
{dog} heard the gas gong before anyone else and started barking. {name} had the mask on in time.
{name} gave {dog} a bath in a shell hole. The dog came out muddier than before and very happy.
{dog} followed {name} on the dawn watch, step for step, ears up the whole time.
The sergeant pretends to hate {dog}. Today the sergeant was seen sharing a biscuit with it.
{dog} brought a dead crow to the dugout as a gift. {name} thanked it and buried the crow outside.
{name} made {dog} a little coat from an old sandbag. The dog looks ridiculous and knows it.
{dog} barked at the enemy line all evening. The enemy line, very politely, did not bark back.
{name} found {dog} sleeping in the machine gun pit. The gunner said it could stay. It is better company than most.
{dog} limped back from no man's land with a piece of enemy bread in its mouth. {name} checked it for wounds. Only mud.
Every man in the squad knows {dog}'s name. Not every man knows the sergeant's.
{dog} waited at the end of the trench until {name} came back from the stores. It always waits.
dogWard: {dog} would not leave the stretcher. The medics stopped trying to send it away and gave it a corner.
{dog} lay beside {name} all day with its head on {his} hand.
The orderly says {dog} has not eaten since {name} was carried in. It just watches the door.
{dog} licked {name}'s face until {he} opened {his} eyes. Then it wagged its whole body.
{dog} sat at the foot of {name}'s bed and growled softly at anyone who came too close. Except the surgeon.
{name} cannot walk yet. {dog} brings {him} things instead: a stick, a glove, a spoon nobody can find.
dogHeir: {dog} the {breed} was waiting at the end of the trench. It sniffed {name} for a long time, then lay down at {his} feet. It stays with the family.
Nobody had the heart to send {dog} away. The {breed} now follows {name}, the same way it followed {prevName}.
{dog} did not eat for two days after {prevName} fell. On the third day it walked up to {name} and sat down. That was that.
dogRename: The squad voted, and the dog will not answer to {oldDog} anymore. From today the {breed} is called {dog}. It wagged at the new name straight away.
{name} decided the dog needed a proper name. {oldDog} is now {dog}. The dog did not seem to mind, as long as dinner still comes.
